cases.title: Post-op day 2: short of breath after therapy

patient.history: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a right tibial plateau fracture 2 days ago after a bicycle crash. Generalized anxiety disorder treated with sertraline. Gender-affirming hormone therapy: oral estradiol, held by the surgeon since admission. Nonsmoker. Full code.

entries.text: POD 2 0800: Alert and oriented. Right leg in hinged brace, toes warm, pink, capillary refill less than 2 seconds. Pain 3/10 at incision. Saline lock in the right forearm, flushed at 0800. Incentive spirometer 1,500 mL. Walked 20 feet with physical therapy (PT) using a walker at 0930.

1015: Called to the room by the client, who is sitting on the edge of the bed after PT. States, 'I suddenly can't catch my breath, and it hurts on the right side when I breathe in.' Speaking in short phrases. Anxious, gripping the bed rail. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Right calf measured 3 cm larger than the left and tender to touch. Incision dressing dry and intact. Pain at the incision 3/10, unchanged. Skin warm and dry.
1030: Rapid response team (RRT) at the bedside. Oxygen 4 L/min by nasal cannula applied. 12-lead ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST elevation. HCP at bedside; CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) prescribed.
1145: CTPA shows a right lower lobe segmental pulmonary embolism. Right ventricle normal size. Troponin within normal limits. HCP prescriptions entered (see Orders).

POD 3 0800: Slept 5 hours. Reports breathing 'much easier' and the right-sided chest pain only when coughing. Right calf circumference unchanged from yesterday. Small bruise, 2 cm, at the abdominal injection site. Urine clear yellow; no blood in urine or stool. States, 'I'm scared I'll get another clot.' Using incentive spirometer, 1,750 mL.

Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous once daily at 0900 (VTE prophylaxis). Oxycodone 5 mg PO every 4 hours PRN moderate pain. Sertraline 100 mg PO daily. Estradiol: on hold per surgeon. PT twice daily, weight bearing as tolerated. Rapid-response standing protocol: oxygen to keep SpO2 92% or higher.

1140: Discontinue enoxaparin 40 mg once daily. Start enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneous every 12 hours (treatment dose, 1 mg/kg rounded to syringe size); first dose now (pharmacy verified timing after the 0905 prophylactic dose). Titrate oxygen to keep SpO2 at or above 92%. Continue to hold estradiol; endocrinology to advise. Platelet count and hemoglobin every morning.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1015 nurses' note and vital signs. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

tokens.text: I suddenly can't catch my breath
it hurts on the right side when I breathe in
Right calf 3 cm larger than the left and tender

rationale.short: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia, tachycardia and a swollen, tender calf on POD 2 are new and dangerous. The low-grade temperature, clear lungs, dry dressing and stable incision pain are not.

h1.text: Key. Sudden dyspnea after the first walk of the day is a classic PE cue.

h2.text: Key. Pleuritic pain points to a pleural process such as an embolism with infarction.

h6.text: Not a key. A low-grade value common after surgery; it does not change the next action.

h7.text: Not a key. Clear lungs make atelectasis or pneumonia less likely; they do not need follow-up themselves.

h8.text: Key. Unilateral calf swelling suggests a DVT, the usual source of a PE.

h10.text: Not a key. Stable surgical pain; not the new problem.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Recognize cues: compare each finding with the client's baseline and expected values; flag what is new, abnormal and dangerous.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 6. Example: selecting 5 keys and 1 distractor earns 5 - 1 = 4 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Compare with the 0800 baseline: a sudden change in breathing after surgery is a clot until proven otherwise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: recognize complications. Trap: treating stable incision pain or a low-grade temperature as the priority cue.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{d1}}. The finding that best argues against a panic attack is {{d2}}. Besides the recent leg surgery, a risk factor for this problem in the client's history is {{d3}}.

rationale.short: The cluster fits a pulmonary embolism. Hypoxemia (SpO2 88%) is what separates it from a panic attack, and estradiol plus recent leg surgery raise the risk.

d1.text: (a) ‘atelectasis’: Not a key. Atelectasis develops gradually, usually with diminished breath sounds; the lungs are clear. (b) ‘a panic attack’: Not a key. Anxiety is present, but panic does not cause hypoxemia or a swollen calf. (c) ‘acute coronary syndrome’: Not a key. Pleuritic pain on breathing in, a swollen calf after leg surgery and hypoxemia with clear lungs fit PE better; ACS still has to be screened with an ECG and troponin. (d) ‘pulmonary embolism’: Key. Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, tachycardia and a swollen calf after leg surgery.

d2.text: (a) ‘SpO2 of 88% on room air’: Key. Hyperventilation from panic keeps SpO2 normal or high; true hypoxemia needs a physical cause. (b) ‘heart rate of 118/min’: Not a key. Tachycardia occurs in panic attacks too. (c) ‘speaking in short phrases’: Not a key. Breathlessness from panic can also shorten speech. (d) ‘respiratory rate of 28/min’: Not a key. Rapid breathing occurs in panic attacks too.

d3.text: (a) ‘sertraline therapy’: Not a key. Sertraline is not a recognized VTE risk factor. (b) ‘anxiety disorder’: Not a key. An anxiety disorder does not raise clot risk; labeling the client 'anxious' is the trap. (c) ‘sulfonamide allergy’: Not a key. An allergy history does not affect clot risk. (d) ‘estradiol therapy’: Key. Estrogen therapy raises VTE risk; recent leg surgery and reduced mobility add to it.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: A known anxiety disorder never explains new hypoxemia.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: identify pathophysiology related to an acute condition. Trap: anchoring on the client's psychiatric history (diagnostic overshadowing).

items.stem: The nurse considers possible causes of the client's change in condition. Select the 2 conditions that are the most immediate threats and must be ruled out first.

rationale.short: Rule out the two killers first: pulmonary embolism and acute coronary syndrome. Panic, atelectasis, infection and opioid effect are less likely or less urgent.

a.text: Not a key. Common after surgery but rarely causes this degree of sudden hypoxemia with clear lungs; not an immediate threat.

b.text: Not a key. Opioids slow breathing; this client is breathing fast.

c.text: Key. Hypoxemia, tachycardia and a swollen calf after leg surgery: life-threatening and most likely.

d.text: Not a key. A diagnosis of exclusion; choosing it first delays care.

e.text: Not a key. The dressing is dry, the temperature is low grade and the onset was sudden.

f.text: Key. Chest pain with tachycardia must be screened with an ECG and troponin even when PE is more likely; both kill quickly.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 2 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 2 choices. Maximum 2. Example: choosing 1 keys and 1 distractor earns 1 of 2.
expanded.takeaway: Prioritize life-threatening explanations before benign ones, even when a benign one is easy to see.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC: prioritize care based on acuity. Trap: picking the most familiar explanation (anxiety) instead of the most dangerous.

items.stem: For each action, choose whether it is indicated or not indicated now.

rows.text: Call the rapid response team
Apply oxygen and titrate to the protocol SpO2 target
Raise the head of the bed to at least 45 degrees
Massage the right calf to relieve the tenderness
Give PRN oxycodone and recheck in 1 hour
Walk the client in the hallway to expand the lungs
Obtain a 12-lead ECG per protocol
Confirm that the IV line is patent

rationale.short: Escalate (RRT), oxygen, upright position, 12-lead ECG and a working IV line. Do not massage the calf, mask the cue with an opioid or walk a hypoxemic client.

r1.text: Indicated. Sudden hypoxemia with tachycardia meets RRT criteria; escalate now (MoC).

r2.text: Indicated. Treats hypoxemia while the cause is confirmed.

r3.text: Indicated. An upright position eases the work of breathing.

r4.text: Not indicated. Massage over a suspected DVT is unsafe and can dislodge clot.

r5.text: Not indicated. Delays escalation and can depress breathing; the pain is a cue, not the problem.

r6.text: Not indicated. Exertion worsens hypoxemia; atelectasis is not the working problem.

r7.text: Indicated. Screens for ACS and documents the rhythm.

r8.text: Indicated. Access is needed for contrast imaging and possible emergency drugs.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 8. Example: one wrong row earns 7 of 8.
expanded.takeaway: In suspected PE, support oxygenation and escalate; the HCP decides imaging and anticoagulation.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC: recognize the need to escalate and obtain orders. Trap: 'walk and use the incentive spirometer' care for presumed atelectasis.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1140 prescriptions and the MAR. Which actions should the nurse take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe before injecting
Confirm the prophylactic 40 mg order is removed from the schedule
Give the first enoxaparin 80 mg dose now as prescribed
Rub the injection site afterward to speed absorption
Teach the client to report blood in urine or black stools
Check the latest platelet count and creatinine before the dose
Hold the first dose until a baseline aPTT result is back

rationale.short: Give the treatment dose now, remove the duplicate prophylactic order, check platelets and creatinine, and teach bleeding signs. Do not expel the bubble, rub the site or wait for an aPTT.

a.text: Not a key. The label says not to expel the bubble; doing so loses drug.

b.text: Key. Two enoxaparin orders at once would double-dose the client; check the MAR.

c.text: Key. The treatment dose (about 1 mg/kg every 12 hours) starts anticoagulation without delay; the HCP and pharmacy accounted for the 0905 prophylactic dose.

d.text: Not a key. Rubbing increases bruising and hematoma.

e.text: Key. Bleeding is the main risk of treatment-dose anticoagulation.

f.text: Key. Baseline platelets (HIT monitoring) and kidney function (enoxaparin is renally cleared) are standard checks.

g.text: Not a key. aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin, not enoxaparin; holding delays treatment.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 4. Example: selecting 3 keys and 1 distractor earns 3 - 1 = 2 of 4.
expanded.takeaway: When the anticoagulant dose changes, look for the old order: duplicate anticoagulants are a top medication error.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PHA: prepare and administer medications using the rights of administration. Trap: aPTT monitoring and air-bubble technique carried over from heparin habits.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the POD 3 0800 assessment. Click to highlight the findings that indicate the client's condition is improving.

tokens.text: 2 cm bruise at the injection site

rationale.short: Lower RR and HR, better SpO2 on less oxygen and easier breathing show improvement. The unchanged calf, small bruise, fear and stable platelets are expected or are separate needs.

h2.text: Key. Better oxygenation on less oxygen than yesterday.

h5.text: Not a key. Expected in the first days of treatment; it is not evidence of improvement.

h6.text: Not a key. A small bruise is expected with enoxaparin; it is not an outcome measure.

h7.text: Not a key. A teaching and coping need, not a sign of improvement.

h8.text: Not a key. A stable platelet count is reassuring for HIT, but it does not show that the embolism is resolving.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Evaluate outcomes: compare new data with the earlier timepoint; decide what improved, what did not and what needs action now.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 4. Example: selecting 3 keys and 1 distractor earns 3 - 1 = 2 of 4.
expanded.takeaway: Evaluate the outcome you were treating (oxygenation and work of breathing), not side findings.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC/PA: evaluate response to treatment. Trap: calling a stable lab or an expected bruise 'improvement'.

cases.title: Step-down night shift: 'I can't get air'

patient.history: Fell from a ladder 2 days ago: right rib fractures 5-7 and a right traumatic pneumothorax. Right chest tube placed in the ED, connected to a dry-suction drainage unit at -20 cm H2O with water seal. Hypertension (amlodipine). Full code.

entries.text: 2200: Chest tube to suction; tidaling present in the water-seal chamber, with intermittent bubbling in the water-seal chamber when the client coughs (small air leak). Breath sounds diminished right base. Subcutaneous crepitus around the insertion site; edge marked with skin marker. Pain 4/10. 2215: Off the unit to CT by portable transport. 2300: Returned from CT; vital signs taken; drowsy, settled for sleep. Chest tube system not reassessed after return.

0200: AP reports the client is 'breathing fast.' Client restless, sitting up, states, 'I can't get air.' Trachea shifted to the left. Breath sounds absent on the right. Neck veins distended at 45 degrees. Heart sounds clear and distinct. Chest tube: a clamp is closed on the tubing 10 cm from the dressing; AP states transport 'clamped it for the trip.' No tidaling and no bubbling in the water-seal chamber. Crepitus now 3 cm beyond the 2200 marked edge; new edge marked at 0200. Drainage serosanguineous, 210 mL total since 1900 (unchanged since 2200). Dressing dry. Pain at the insertion site 4/10, unchanged.
0205: Rapid response called. Charge nurse at bedside.
0215: Clamp released at 0206; rush of bubbling in the water-seal chamber. Nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min. HCP at bedside at 0210.

0240: Trachea midline. Neck veins flat at 45 degrees. Breath sounds now heard in the right upper lobe, faint at the right base. Water-seal chamber shows tidaling with breathing and intermittent bubbling on exhalation. Crepitus edge unchanged from the 0200 marking. Client states, 'I can breathe again.' Portable chest x-ray read by HCP at 0235: right lung re-expanded except a small apical rim; tube in good position.

Chest tube to -20 cm H2O suction. Do not clamp. Chest x-ray daily. Oxygen to keep SpO2 at or above 92%. Hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV every 3 hours PRN severe pain. Incentive spirometer every hour while awake.

references.locator: never clamp a bubbling chest drain; clamping only under specialist supervision

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0200 nurses' note. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

tokens.text: Breath sounds absent on the right
a clamp is closed on the tubing
No tidaling in the water-seal chamber

rationale.short: Tracheal shift, absent breath sounds, distended neck veins, a closed clamp and no tidaling are the dangerous cluster. Clear heart sounds, stable drainage, a dry dressing and site pain are not the emergency.

h1.text: Key. Shift away from the injured side signals rising pressure in the right chest.

h2.text: Key. The right lung has collapsed further.

h3.text: Key. Raised intrathoracic pressure is blocking venous return.

h4.text: Not a key. Argues against pericardial tamponade.

h5.text: Key. The tube was never unclamped after transport: air cannot leave the pleural space.

h6.text: Key. No swing means no communication with the pleural space, here because of the clamp.

h7.text: Not a key. Expected and unchanged; does not suggest new bleeding.

h9.text: Not a key. Same as at 2200; treat later, it is not the life threat.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Recognize cues: compare each finding with the client's baseline and expected values; flag what is new, abnormal and dangerous.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 5. Example: selecting 4 keys and 1 distractor earns 4 - 1 = 3 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: A clamped chest tube plus falling BP is a tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan RRP: recognize complications of a drainage device. Trap: focusing on drainage volume or pain.

items.stem: Two conditions can cause shock with full neck veins. For each finding, choose which condition it supports.

columns.label: Supports tension pneumothorax over cardiac tamponade

rows.text: Trachea deviated toward the left side
No air movement heard over the right chest
Neck veins full at 45 degrees
BP 86/58 mm Hg with HR 128/min
Heart tones crisp, not muffled
Temperature 37.2 °C (37.1 °C at 2300)

rationale.short: Shock and distended neck veins fit both tamponade and tension pneumothorax; tracheal shift, absent unilateral breath sounds and crisp (not muffled) heart tones point to tension pneumothorax. A normal temperature fits neither.

r1.text: Supports tension pneumothorax over cardiac tamponade. Mediastinal shift happens with tension pneumothorax, not tamponade.

r2.text: Supports tension pneumothorax over cardiac tamponade. Lung collapse is unilateral in pneumothorax; tamponade spares breath sounds.

r3.text: Consistent with both conditions. Both obstruct venous return to the heart.

r4.text: Consistent with both conditions. Both cause obstructive shock.

r5.text: Supports tension pneumothorax over cardiac tamponade. Tamponade muffles heart sounds, so crisp heart tones argue against tamponade and support tension pneumothorax as the cause.

r6.text: Supports neither condition. A normal, stable temperature does not point to either condition.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Breath sounds and trachea position separate the two obstructive shocks.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan RRP/PA: identify pathophysiology. Trap: stopping at 'shock with JVD' without finding the discriminating cue.

items.stem: Select the 2 client problems that pose the greatest immediate threat.

options.text: Acute pain at the chest-tube insertion site, rated 4/10
Hypoxemia from collapse of the right lung
Anxiety and restlessness about being unable to breathe
Risk for infection at the chest-tube insertion site
Spreading subcutaneous emphysema beyond the marked edge
Obstructive shock from trapped pleural air

rationale.short: Shock and hypoxemia from the trapped air come first. Subcutaneous emphysema, pain, infection risk and anxiety can wait.

a.text: Not a key. Treat after the airway, breathing and circulation problem.

b.text: Key. SpO2 84% on 4 L/min with RR 34/min: breathing is failing.

c.text: Not a key. Restlessness here is from hypoxemia; treating 'anxiety' misses the cause.

d.text: Not a key. A potential problem; actual problems come first.

e.text: Not a key. Uncomfortable and a sign of the air leak, but not itself the threat.

f.text: Key. BP 86/58 with distended neck veins: circulation is failing.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 2 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 2 choices. Maximum 2. Example: choosing 1 keys and 1 distractor earns 1 of 2.
expanded.takeaway: Restlessness in a hypoxemic client is a breathing problem, not a behavior problem.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC: prioritize by ABCs. Trap: choosing the most visible finding (crepitus) instead of the lethal one.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Give the PRN hydromorphone before any other action
Strip the tubing toward the drainage unit to clear it
Release the clamp on the chest-tube tubing
Lower the head of the bed flat to rest the heart
Raise the wall suction to -40 cm H2O to remove more air

rationale.short: Unclamp the tube, give high-flow oxygen and call the RRT. Do not strip, raise suction, lie the client flat or give an opioid first.

a.text: Key. If releasing the clamp does not fix it, the HCP must decompress the chest.

b.text: Key. Treats severe hypoxemia while the problem is fixed.

c.text: Not a key. An opioid can depress breathing and delays the fix.

d.text: Not a key. There are no clots; stripping creates high negative pressure and is not recommended.

e.text: Key. Reopens the path for trapped air; the prescription says do not clamp.

f.text: Not a key. Flat positioning worsens breathing.

g.text: Not a key. Does nothing while the tube is clamped and can injure the lung; changing suction needs a prescription.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 3. Example: selecting 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 - 1 = 1 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Clamps belong at the bedside, not on the tube.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan RRP: manage drainage devices. Trap: stripping/milking and 'more suction' myths.

items.stem: For each action, specify whether the nurse should do it now, it requires the HCP, or it is not appropriate.

rows.text: Reassess breath sounds, trachea and BP right after the system is reopened
Perform needle or finger thoracostomy if tension persists after the tube is reopened
Insert a new chest tube if the reopened tube does not drain
Place the thoracostomy tray and sterile supplies at the bedside
Reapply the clamp before the portable chest x-ray
Ask the AP to recheck the vital signs and report back in 15 minutes

rationale.short: The RN reassesses at the bedside and readies supplies; the HCP decompresses or replaces the tube if needed. Re-clamping or handing an unstable client to the AP is unsafe.

r1.text: Nurse does now. Immediate reassessment shows whether the fix worked or decompression is needed.

r2.text: Requires the HCP. Invasive decompression is a provider procedure.

r3.text: Requires the HCP. Provider procedure if the current tube has failed.

r4.text: Nurse does now. Preparing for decompression saves minutes.

r5.text: Not appropriate. Clamping caused the problem; x-rays do not require clamping.

r6.text: Not appropriate. The client is unstable; the RN stays and reassesses continuously.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0240 findings. For each finding, choose the one column that best describes what it shows.

columns.label: Air is leaving the chest and the lung is re-expanding
Venous return and BP are recovering

rows.text: Chest x-ray: right lung re-expanded except a small apical rim
Breath sounds heard in the right upper lobe
Intermittent bubbling on exhalation
BP 122/74 mm Hg (was 86/58)
Neck veins flat at 45 degrees (were distended)
Crepitus edge the same as the edge marked at 0200

rationale.short: A re-expanded lung on x-ray, returning breath sounds and bubbling on exhalation show air is leaving the chest and the lung is re-expanding. The better BP and flat neck veins show venous return has recovered. The crepitus has not spread but is unchanged.

r1.text: Air is leaving the chest and the lung is re-expanding. The pleural air has largely been evacuated through the tube.

r2.text: Air is leaving the chest and the lung is re-expanding. Air is moving into the re-expanding lung.

r3.text: Air is leaving the chest and the lung is re-expanding. Air is leaving the pleural space through the reopened tube, as expected with the known small leak.

r4.text: Venous return and BP are recovering. With pressure off the heart and great veins, cardiac output and BP have recovered.

r5.text: Venous return and BP are recovering. Venous return to the heart is no longer blocked.

r6.text: Unchanged from 0200. Subcutaneous air has not spread past the 0200 mark but has not cleared; keep marking and checking it.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Evaluate outcomes: compare new data with the earlier timepoint; decide what improved, what did not and what needs action now.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: After unclamping, expect tidaling and some bubbling; continuous bubbling with no breathing pattern suggests a system leak.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan RRP: evaluate response to a procedure. Trap: thinking any bubbling means the system has failed.

cases.title: Day after PCI: 'I feel like I'm going to pass out'

patient.history: Inferior ST-elevation MI 18 hours ago; drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery through the right radial artery. Type 2 diabetes (metformin held). Hyperlipidemia. Full code.

entries.text: 0600: Sinus rhythm 72/min, PR 0.22 s, QRS 0.08 s. Denies chest pain. Right radial site soft, no hematoma, radial pulse 2+.

0905: Monitor alarm. Client in bed, states, 'I feel like I'm going to pass out.' Skin cool and clammy. Oriented but slow to answer. Rhythm strip: atrial rate 78/min, regular, with some P waves hidden in QRS complexes or T waves; ventricular rate 40/min, regular; PR intervals vary with no repeating pattern; QRS 0.10 s. Denies chest pain. Reports a mild backache from lying in bed. Right radial site soft, no hematoma.

0915: Rapid response team at bedside. Atropine 1 mg IV given at 0910. Monitor at 0915: atrial rate 80/min, ventricular rate 42/min, PR intervals still varying. Transcutaneous pacing pads on. HCP at bedside; new prescriptions entered.

0945: Transcutaneous pacing at 70/min since 0920; output 80 mA. Monitor: a wide QRS follows each pacer spike. Femoral pulse 70/min. Alert and oriented, no dizziness. Grimacing, rates pain under the pads 7/10 ('burning, twitching'); no chest pain. Fentanyl 25 mcg IV given at 0922 (next PRN dose available at 0952). Urine output 20 mL since 0845. Cardiology en route for transvenous pacemaker.

tabs.label: MAR
rows: Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg PO every 12 h
Fentanyl 25 mcg IV now, then every 30 min PRN pacing discomfort

entries.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring. Up in room with assistance. Notify HCP for HR below 50/min or SBP below 90 mm Hg.

0914 prescriptions: Begin transcutaneous pacing at 70/min; increase output until capture. Fentanyl 25 mcg IV now as pacing begins, then every 30 minutes PRN pacing discomfort. Page cardiology now for transvenous pacemaker. Epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min IV if pacing fails to capture. Hold metoprolol. Ticagrelor 90 mg PO at 2000; continue dual antiplatelet therapy. Atorvastatin 80 mg PO at bedtime. Cardiac rehabilitation referral before discharge. Bed rest starting now until transvenous pacemaker placed.

references.locator: early oral beta-blocker: avoid with PR >0.24 s or 2nd/3rd-degree AV block

items.stem: Look at each 0905 finding. Does it fit complete heart block only, or both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia?

columns.label: Both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia

rows.text: Ventricular rate 40/min
Atrial rate 78/min while the ventricular rate is 40/min
PR intervals vary with no repeating pattern
Some P waves hidden in QRS complexes or T waves
QRS 0.10 s
Regular R-R intervals
Hypotension with near-syncope

rationale.short: An atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate, varying PR intervals and P waves hidden in QRS or T waves point to complete heart block. A slow regular rate, a narrow QRS and hypotension fit both.

r1.text: Both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia. Both rhythms can be this slow.

r2.text: Complete heart block only. In sinus bradycardia every P wave is followed by a QRS, so the rates match.

r3.text: Complete heart block only. Atria and ventricles beat independently. Sinus bradycardia has a constant PR interval.

r4.text: Complete heart block only. P waves march through at their own rate, unrelated to the QRS.

r5.text: Both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia. A narrow QRS fits sinus bradycardia and a junctional escape rhythm from the AV node region.

r6.text: Both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia. A junctional escape rhythm is regular, as is sinus bradycardia.

r7.text: Both complete heart block and sinus bradycardia. Either rhythm can cause poor perfusion when slow enough.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 7. Example: one wrong row earns 6 of 7.
expanded.takeaway: Compare the P rate with the QRS rate: when they differ and the PR keeps changing, the AV node is not conducting.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: interpret rhythm cues. Trap: calling any slow regular rhythm sinus bradycardia.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{d1}} related to {{d2}}, which places the client at greatest risk for {{d3}}.

options.text: a vagal response to back pain
a toxic effect of the 0800 metoprolol dose
loss of AV node conduction after inferior MI

rationale.short: Decreased cardiac output from loss of AV conduction after an inferior MI is the priority problem, and the escape rhythm can fail into cardiac arrest.

d1.text: (a) ‘fluid volume overload’: Not a key. No crackles, edema or weight gain. (b) ‘decreased cardiac output’: Key. A ventricular rate of 40/min cannot keep the BP up. (c) ‘bleeding from the access site’: Not a key. The radial site is soft with no hematoma. (d) ‘hypoglycemia’: Not a key. Glucose is 146 mg/dL.

d2.text: (a) ‘fluid loss from contrast-induced diuresis’: Not a key. Would cause a fast, not slow, heart rate. (b) ‘a vagal response to back pain’: Not a key. A vagal response slows the sinus node; the P waves here are 78/min. (c) ‘a toxic effect of the 0800 metoprolol dose’: Not a key. One 25 mg dose given with a PR of 0.22 s does not explain new complete AV dissociation the day after an inferior MI; the ischemic AV node does. (d) ‘loss of AV node conduction after inferior MI’: Key. The right coronary artery usually supplies the AV node; the narrow junctional escape fits a block at the node.

d3.text: (a) ‘cardiac arrest’: Key. An unreliable escape rhythm can fail; this is the immediate danger. (b) ‘hyperkalemia’: Not a key. Potassium is normal. (c) ‘stent thrombosis’: Not a key. A risk after PCI, but the client is taking dual antiplatelet therapy, and it is not what this rhythm threatens. (d) ‘heart failure in 6 months’: Not a key. A later concern, not the immediate one.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Inferior MI plus new block means the AV node is ischemic; prepare to pace.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize by acuity. Trap: blaming a routine drug dose and waiting for it to wear off.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the client to bear down as if having a bowel movement
Help the client walk to the bathroom
Keep the client in bed until the rhythm is treated
Place transcutaneous pacing pads on the chest
Prepare adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Prepare atropine 1 mg IV per protocol
Hold the next metoprolol dose and notify the HCP

rationale.short: Place pacing pads, prepare atropine, call the RRT, hold metoprolol and keep the client in bed. Vagal maneuvers, adenosine and walking are wrong for a slow rhythm.

a.text: Not a key. The Valsalva maneuver slows the heart rate; it is a tachycardia maneuver.

b.text: Not a key. The client is near syncope; standing risks a fall and arrest.

c.text: Not a key. Vagal maneuvers slow the heart more.

d.text: Key. Near-syncope makes standing unsafe.

e.text: Key. Hypotension with near-syncope needs emergency help.

f.text: Key. Pads must be ready in case atropine fails; pacing must not be delayed in an unstable client.

g.text: Not a key. Adenosine blocks the AV node; it is for SVT.

h.text: Key. First-line drug for unstable bradycardia while pacing is set up.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 5. Example: selecting 4 keys and 1 distractor earns 4 - 1 = 3 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then pacing; get the pads on early.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PHA/PA: choose interventions for a dysrhythmia. Trap: carrying over tachycardia interventions.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0915 note and vital signs and the 0914 prescriptions. Click to highlight the prescriptions the nurse should carry out immediately.

tokens.text: Begin transcutaneous pacing at 70/min; increase output until capture
Fentanyl 25 mcg IV now as pacing begins, then every 30 minutes PRN pacing discomfort
Page cardiology now for transvenous pacemaker
Epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min IV if pacing fails to capture
Ticagrelor 90 mg PO at 2000; continue dual antiplatelet therapy
Bed rest starting now until transvenous pacemaker placed

rationale.short: The 0915 data show atropine failed (rate 42/min, BP 80/48). Start pacing, give fentanyl for pacing pain, page cardiology now and keep the client on bed rest. The epinephrine order is conditional, and the remaining orders are routine.

h1.text: Key. Atropine has failed: 5 minutes after the dose the ventricular rate is 42/min and the BP is 80/48. Pacing is the next step in unstable bradycardia.

h2.text: Key. The first dose is ordered now: pacing is painful, and analgesia is given when feasible without delaying pacing.

h3.text: Key. Transcutaneous pacing is a bridge.

h4.text: Not a key. Conditional; pacing has not been tried yet.

h5.text: Not a key. Continue at the scheduled time; not urgent. Ticagrelor can cause bradyarrhythmias (label warning), so cardiology may review it, but stopping antiplatelet therapy the day after a stent risks stent thrombosis.

h8.text: Key. Takes effect now: a paced client with a failing escape rhythm must not get up.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 4. Example: selecting 3 keys and 1 distractor earns 3 - 1 = 2 of 4.
expanded.takeaway: When atropine fails, pace; treat the pain the pacing causes.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA/MOC: carry out emergency prescriptions in order of priority. Trap: running the conditional infusion first.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0945 findings. For each finding, choose the one column that best describes what it shows.

rows.text: A wide QRS follows each pacer spike
Femoral pulse 70/min, matching the pacer rate
BP 108/66 mm Hg
Alert and oriented, no dizziness
Rates pain under the pads 7/10 (burning, twitching)
Urine output 20 mL since 0845

rationale.short: Spikes followed by wide QRS show electrical capture; a matching femoral pulse confirms mechanical capture. BP and mental status show perfusion. Pain 7/10 and low urine output still need action.

r1.text: Confirms pacer capture (rhythm or pulse). Electrical capture; it does not prove the heart is pumping, so confirm a pulse.

r2.text: Confirms pacer capture (rhythm or pulse). Mechanical capture is confirmed with a pulse at the pacer rate, checked at the femoral site to avoid confusing muscle twitching with a pulse.

r3.text: Shows organ perfusion (BP, brain). The pressure is now high enough to perfuse the organs.

r4.text: Shows organ perfusion (BP, brain). The brain is perfused.

r5.text: Needs nursing action now. The next PRN fentanyl dose is not due until 0952: reassess, ask the HCP about added analgesia or sedation, and confirm output is not set higher than needed for capture.

r6.text: Needs nursing action now. About 0.2 mL/kg/h; report and monitor hourly.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Evaluate outcomes: compare new data with the earlier timepoint; decide what improved, what did not and what needs action now.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Electrical capture is not enough; confirm a pulse at the pacer rate.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: evaluate pacing. Trap: equating pacer spikes on the monitor with perfusion.

cases.title: Oncology unit evening: new fever after a transfusion

patient.history: Left breast cancer. Dose-dense doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, cycle 2, day 10; pegfilgrastim given on day 2. Implanted single-lumen chest port. Admitted yesterday for dehydration from mouth sores and poor intake. Received 1 unit of packed red blood cells today, 1300-1530, with no reaction. Full code.

entries.text: 1530: Transfusion complete; vital signs before, during and after within baseline. 1800: Ate half of a soft dinner. Mouth sores rated 2/10 with prescribed mouth rinse. Port site clean and dry, no redness.

2010: Client reports chills and feeling 'achy all over.' Alert and oriented. Lungs clear. Port site without redness, swelling or drainage. No cough, no urinary burning. Mouth sores unchanged. Hair loss noted on pillow. Urine output 40 mL/h over the last 4 hours.
2025: HCP notified using SBAR; prescriptions received (see Orders).

Next day 0600: Slept in short naps. Port tunnel: new 3 cm area of redness and tenderness along the catheter path above the port. Lungs clear. Urine output 50 mL/h over 8 hours. Preliminary blood culture result called by the laboratory at 0540 (see Labs).
Vital signs every 4 hours. Notify HCP for temperature 38.0 °C or higher. Ondansetron 8 mg PO every 8 hours PRN nausea. Mouth rinse every 4 hours. Standard precautions.

2025: Blood cultures x 2 sets (1 set from the port, 1 set from a peripheral vein). Cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours, first dose now. Lactate now. Lactated Ringer's 1,000 mL IV over 1 hour. Chest x-ray (portable). Urinalysis and urine culture.

cases.revealRule: Chart content tagged with a time point is shown only when the student reaches an item at or after that time point; 'baseline' is shown from the start. Tables use rowTimepoints or columnTimepoints (the latest applicable tag wins).

rationale.short: Fever with an ANC of 300 plus a rising heart rate and falling BP need action now. The hemoglobin, platelets, mouth sores and hair loss are expected or stable.

c.text: Not a key. Expected after 1 unit; not the urgent problem.

items.stem: Is each statement about the client accurate or inaccurate?

rows.text: Her temperature meets the definition of fever in a client with neutropenia
A port site with no redness or drainage rules out a line infection
The rising heart rate and falling BP suggest sepsis may be developing
The fever can wait for the morning CBC
Her low neutrophil count may hide the usual signs of infection
Clear lungs rule out pneumonia

rationale.short: Fever plus neutropenia is an emergency, and early sepsis is likely. Normal-looking sites and clear lungs do not rule out infection because neutropenia hides inflammation.

r1.text: Accurate. A single oral reading of 38.3 °C or higher counts.

r2.text: Inaccurate. Without neutrophils, redness and pus may not form.

r3.text: Accurate. Both changed from her 1530 baseline.

r4.text: Inaccurate. Fever with neutropenia is treated as an emergency now.

r5.text: Accurate. Neutropenia blunts inflammation.

r6.text: Inaccurate. Pneumonia may have few findings in neutropenia; imaging is still needed.

expanded.takeaway: Absent local signs mean little in a client without neutrophils.

chills starting 4 hours 40 minutes after the RBC transfusion ended
urine output of 40 mL/h with poor oral intake
a temperature of 38.4 °C with an ANC of 300/µL
a fever that began after a blood transfusion
mouth sores that limited intake before admission

rationale.short: Sepsis from an infection is most likely: febrile neutropenia (38.4 °C with ANC 300/µL) with a falling BP. A transfusion reaction is unlikely 4 hours 40 minutes after a reaction-free transfusion ended (1530 to 2010).

c.text: (a) ‘a febrile transfusion reaction’: Not a key. The transfusion ended 4 hours 40 minutes earlier with normal vital signs throughout. (b) ‘sepsis from an infection’: Key. Fever with neutropenia, tachycardia and falling BP. (c) ‘dehydration from poor intake’: Not a key. Dehydration does not explain a fever of 38.4 °C with chills. (d) ‘tumor lysis syndrome’: Not a key. Unlikely in breast cancer on day 10; no electrolyte changes.

e1.text: (a) ‘hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL after 1 unit of RBCs’: Not a key. Expected after the transfusion; not evidence of infection. (b) ‘BP falling from 118/74 to 100/60 mm Hg’: Key. Early hypoperfusion. (c) ‘chills starting 4 hours 40 minutes after the RBC transfusion ended’: Not a key. Would point to a transfusion reaction, but febrile reactions occur during or within about 4 hours of a reaction-free transfusion. (d) ‘urine output of 40 mL/h with poor oral intake’: Not a key. Would point to dehydration, but this output is adequate and intake was improving.

e2.text: (a) ‘a temperature of 38.4 °C with an ANC of 300/µL’: Key. Meets the definition of febrile neutropenia: a single oral temperature of 38.3 °C or higher with ANC below 500/µL. (b) ‘a fever that began after a blood transfusion’: Not a key. Timing alone does not make it a transfusion reaction; the vital signs were normal throughout and for hours afterward. (c) ‘mouth sores that limited intake before admission’: Not a key. The reason for admission; does not explain fever with a falling BP tonight. (d) ‘a potassium of 3.9 mEq/L’: Not a key. Normal; argues against tumor lysis rather than for sepsis.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and recheck in 1 hour before calling
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to track output
Plan to give the first IV antibiotic within 1 hour
Notify the HCP now using SBAR
Place the client on droplet precautions
Plan blood cultures from the port and a vein
Take a rectal temperature to confirm the fever

rationale.short: Call the HCP, plan cultures from the port and a vein, give the first antibiotic within 1 hour and check lactate. Rectal temperatures, waiting on acetaminophen, droplet precautions and a catheter are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. Delays antibiotics and masks the fever.

b.text: Key. Lactate helps judge how severe the sepsis is.

c.text: Not a key. Adds an infection risk; output can be measured without it.

d.text: Key. Every hour of delay raises the risk of death.

e.text: Key. Fever in neutropenia needs prescriptions now.

f.text: Not a key. No respiratory droplet illness is suspected; standard precautions and hand hygiene apply.

g.text: Key. Cultures from both sites help find a line infection; draw them before the first dose.

h.text: Not a key. Rectal routes are avoided in neutropenia (mucosal injury, infection).

cases.title: Heart failure admission: monitor alarm

patient.history: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30%). Admitted 2 days ago for volume overload; receiving IV furosemide. No implanted defibrillator (evaluation planned). Hypertension. Full code.

entries.text: 1300: Monitor alarm 'V-tach' while client brushing her teeth at the sink. On the strip, regular narrow QRS complexes at 78/min are visible through the irregular baseline. SpO2 waveform shows pulse rate 78/min. Client denies symptoms; BP 112/70 mm Hg. Lead re-secured; alarm cleared.

1410: Monitor alarm. Client in bed, states, 'My chest feels tight and I feel like I might faint.' Skin cool and pale. Slow to answer but oriented. Monitor: regular wide-complex rhythm at 180/min in leads II and V1. Radial pulse weak, 180/min. Lungs: fine crackles at both bases, unchanged from morning.

1414: Pads applied; sedation being drawn up for synchronized cardioversion. 1416: Before cardioversion could be delivered, the client became unresponsive. No breathing, no pulse. Monitor: wide-complex rhythm at 190/min. Code called; team arriving with the defibrillator already at the bedside.

1440: Unsynchronized shocks at 1417 and 1419 with CPR between; epinephrine 1 mg IV at 1419 after the second shock. Return of spontaneous circulation at 1421 (sudden EtCO2 rise, then pulse confirmed). Intubated at 1426. Norepinephrine 4 mcg/min started at 1424 for MAP 58; weaned off at 1438. Right internal jugular central venous catheter placed by the HCP at 1430; tip position confirmed on portable chest x-ray at 1436. Does not follow commands. Monitor: sinus tachycardia 108/min with occasional PVCs (now 8/min, up from 4/min at 1435). Carotid pulse strong.
Furosemide 40 mg IV every 12 hours. Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO twice daily. Continuous cardiac monitoring. Daily weight. Notify HCP of sustained dysrhythmia.

1438: Titrate FiO2 to SpO2 90-98%. Keep MAP at or above 65 mm Hg; restart norepinephrine if MAP falls below 65. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 15 minutes. Potassium chloride 10 mEq/h IV via central line x 4 doses. 12-lead ECG now. Temperature control per protocol: prevent fever and keep 32-37.5 °C for at least 36 hours.

references.locator: shock -> CPR 2 min -> shock -> CPR + epinephrine every 3-5 min -> shock -> CPR + amiodarone
Sec 4.1 FiO2 titrated to SpO2 90-98%; Sec 5 MAP >=65 mm Hg; Sec 7 temperature control 32-37.5 C >=36 h if not following commands

items.stem: The nurse assesses the client at 1410. Select the 3 findings that are signs of poor perfusion showing the client is unstable.

options.text: Wide QRS complexes in leads II and V1
Fine crackles at both bases, unchanged since morning
'I feel like I might faint' and slow to answer

rationale.short: Hypotension, ischemic chest discomfort and signs of poor brain perfusion define instability. The rate, QRS width, potassium and unchanged crackles do not.

a.text: Not a key. Describes the rhythm, not the client's stability.

b.text: Not a key. Unchanged from the morning; not new acute heart failure.

c.text: Key. Hypotension is a sign of instability: MAP (86 + 2 x 50) / 3 = 62, below 65.

d.text: Key. Signs of poor brain perfusion.

e.text: Key. Ischemic chest discomfort is a sign of instability.

f.text: Not a key. AHA 2025 defines instability by the client's signs (hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure). A rate of 150 or more makes the rhythm the likely cause of those signs, but the monitor rate is not itself a sign of poor perfusion.

g.text: Not a key. A likely trigger, not a sign of instability.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Recognize cues: compare each finding with the client's baseline and expected values; flag what is new, abnormal and dangerous.

expanded.takeaway: Stability is judged by the client's signs, not by the monitor.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: recognize instability. Trap: calling a fast rate 'unstable' by itself.

items.stem: The nurse compares the 1300 and 1410 monitor alarms. For each finding, specify whether it supports a true dysrhythmia or artifact.

rows.text: 1410: radial pulse 180/min, matching the monitor rate
1410: wide complexes in both leads II and V1

1300: alarm while brushing teeth, with no symptoms

rationale.short: At 1410 a matching pulse, the rhythm in 2 leads and symptoms show true VT. At 1300 normal complexes under the noise, brushing teeth, no symptoms and an SpO2 rate of 78/min show artifact.

r1.text: True dysrhythmia. A matching pulse confirms the rhythm is real.

r2.text: True dysrhythmia. Artifact usually appears in one lead; a real rhythm shows in all.

r3.text: Artifact. The underlying rhythm continues under the noise.

r4.text: Artifact. Arm movement creates artifact.

r5.text: True dysrhythmia. A real rhythm causes symptoms.

r6.text: Artifact. The pulse oximeter rate does not match the alarm rate.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: At 1410 the client has {{d1}}, so the priority treatment is {{d2}} because {{d3}}.

options.text: artifact from movement on the monitor
the QRS complexes are wider than 0.12 s
she has a pulse, low BP and chest pain
her potassium this morning was 3.4 mEq/L

rationale.short: Unstable VT with a pulse calls for synchronized cardioversion because of the hypotension and chest discomfort. Defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; drugs are for stable VT.

d1.text: (a) ‘unstable ventricular tachycardia’: Key. Wide, regular, 180/min with a pulse and signs of instability. (b) ‘stable ventricular tachycardia’: Not a key. She has hypotension and chest discomfort. (c) ‘artifact from movement on the monitor’: Not a key. The pulse matches the monitor. (d) ‘sinus tachycardia from heart failure’: Not a key. The QRS is wide and the rate is 180/min.

d2.text: (a) ‘unsynchronized defibrillation’: Not a key. Used only when there is no pulse. (b) ‘adenosine IV push’: Not a key. For regular narrow-complex SVT. (c) ‘an amiodarone infusion alone’: Not a key. Drugs are for stable VT; unstable VT needs a shock. (d) ‘synchronized cardioversion’: Key. Unstable VT with a pulse is treated with a synchronized shock.

d3.text: (a) ‘the QRS complexes are wider than 0.12 s’: Not a key. Width defines VT but not stability. (b) ‘she has a pulse, low BP and chest pain’: Key. These signs drive the choice of an immediate synchronized shock. (c) ‘the heart rate is above 150/min’: Not a key. Rate alone does not decide the treatment. (d) ‘her potassium this morning was 3.4 mEq/L’: Not a key. Replace it, but potassium does not choose the treatment.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Pulse plus instability = synchronized; no pulse = unsynchronized.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize treatment by stability. Trap: mixing up synchronized and unsynchronized shocks.

Turn on the synchronize mode before the shock
Prepare adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a flush
Wait for a 12-lead ECG before giving any treatment

rationale.short: Call for help and the defibrillator, apply pads, synchronize and sedate if feasible. Vagal maneuvers, adenosine and waiting for an ECG are wrong; IV push potassium is fatal.

a.text: Not a key. IV push potassium is never given; it can cause cardiac arrest.

b.text: Key. A shock will be needed.

c.text: Not a key. A vagal maneuver will not stop VT and wastes time.

d.text: Key. Pads allow a shock without delay.

e.text: Key. Sedate when feasible, but do not delay the shock.

f.text: Key. Synchronization avoids a shock on the T wave.

g.text: Not a key. Adenosine is not for unstable wide-complex VT.

h.text: Not a key. Do not delay treatment of an unstable client.

rows.text: EtCO2 rose suddenly from 18 to 42 mm Hg
Potassium 3.2 mEq/L and magnesium 1.4 mg/dL
Strong carotid pulse
Saturation 100% on FiO2 1.0
PVCs now 8/min, up from 4/min
MAP 73 mm Hg with norepinephrine weaned off

rationale.short: The EtCO2 jump, a strong pulse and a MAP of 73 off vasopressors show effective resuscitation. Low potassium and magnesium, a saturation of 100% on pure oxygen and rising PVCs need follow-up now.

r1.text: Shows effective resuscitation. A sudden rise is an early sign of ROSC.

r2.text: Needs follow-up now. Low levels can trigger VT again; give the prescribed replacement.

r3.text: Shows effective resuscitation. Circulation has returned.

r4.text: Needs follow-up now. Oxygenation is adequate, but too much oxygen is harmful after arrest: titrate FiO2 down to SpO2 90-98% now.

r5.text: Needs follow-up now. Rising ectopy is a warning sign; report.

r6.text: Shows effective resuscitation. Meets the AHA 2025 goal of MAP 65 mm Hg or more without a vasopressor.

cases.title: L&D triage: bleeding on waking

patient.history: G3 P2, 33 0/7 weeks by first-trimester ultrasound. Two prior cesarean births. Ultrasound at 20 weeks: placenta low-lying; follow-up scan at 28 weeks was not done (moved to a new city). Blood type O positive. Smokes 5 cigarettes a day.

entries.text: 0640: Arrived by car. Woke at 0530 in a pool of bright red blood. States, 'It doesn't hurt at all.' Has soaked 2 full-size pads in the last hour (pads brought in: 190 g total; each dry pad weighs 10 g). Uterus soft and nontender between tightenings. Irregular mild tightening at 10- to 15-minute intervals. Fetal movement felt this morning. Fetus in breech presentation by Leopold maneuvers. Membranes intact.

0700: Fetal monitor applied at 0645 (see Fetal Monitoring). Blood drawn by venipuncture at 0650; hemoglobin and platelets resulted at 0658, fibrinogen pending. Still bleeding bright red: the pad applied at 0640 weighs 45 g at 0700 (dry weight 10 g). HR 112/min. Uterus soft and nontender. HCP paged for bedside ultrasound.

0720: Bedside ultrasound by HCP: placenta previa covering the internal cervical os, on the lower uterine segment over the prior cesarean scars. Bleeding slowed to a small amount on pad. Admitted to antepartum for monitoring; prescriptions entered.

0750: Targeted ultrasound by maternal-fetal medicine (MFM): no sonographic signs of placenta accreta spectrum; MFM, anesthesia and blood bank aware of previa with 2 prior cesareans. 1300: Bleeding now spotting only; 1 pad in 4 hours (weighed 18 g; dry weight 10 g). Uterus soft. No contractions in 2 hours. Fetal movement felt. Client tearful: 'Is my baby going to come early?' Has not yet met the neonatal team. Betamethasone dose 1 given at 0745. One 18-gauge IV in the left forearm; the second ordered IV line was not placed (attempt failed at 0730).

0720: Admit to antepartum. Pelvic rest; no digital cervical exams. Continuous EFM. Two 18-gauge IV lines. Type and crossmatch 4 units RBCs. Betamethasone injectable suspension 12 mg every 24 hours x 2 doses, first dose now. Quantify blood loss by weighing pads. CBC every 6 hours. NPO except sips until bleeding stops for 12 hours. Neonatal team consult. MFM consult for placenta accreta spectrum evaluation and delivery planning.

references.locator: previa with 2 prior cesareans: PAS risk about 11%; targeted imaging; multidisciplinary planning; blood availability

items.stem: For each finding, does it suggest previa over abruption, or not?

columns.label: Does not suggest previa over abruption

rows.text: Bleeding with no pain
Uterus soft and nontender between tightenings
Low-lying placenta on the 20-week ultrasound
Bright red rather than dark red blood
Smokes 5 cigarettes a day
Maternal HR 108/min

rationale.short: Painless bleeding, a soft uterus, a low-lying placenta at 20 weeks and bright red blood point to previa. Smoking and a raised heart rate do not suggest previa over abruption (smoking, if anything, leans toward abruption).

r1.text: Suggests previa over abruption. Abruption is usually painful.

r2.text: Suggests previa over abruption. Abruption often causes a firm, tender uterus.

r3.text: Suggests previa over abruption. A placenta that started low and was never rechecked can still cover the cervix.

r4.text: Suggests previa over abruption. Previa bleeding comes from the open placental edge at the cervix and drains out at once, so it is bright red; abruption bleeding collects behind the placenta and is usually dark.

r5.text: Does not suggest previa over abruption. Smoking raises the risk of both, and more for abruption (pooled odds ratio about 1.8-1.9) than for previa (about 1.4-1.6), so it does not suggest previa over abruption.

r6.text: Does not suggest previa over abruption. Any significant blood loss raises the heart rate.

expanded.takeaway: Pain and uterine tone separate previa (painless, soft) from abruption (painful, firm).

items.stem: At 0700 the nurse reviews the new findings. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client's most immediate risk is {{c}} because of {{e}}.

options.text: smoking 5 cigarettes a day during pregnancy
ongoing bleeding, a rising HR and a falling Hgb
a fetus in breech presentation at 33 weeks

rationale.short: Hemorrhagic shock is the greatest risk: at 0700 bleeding continues, the heart rate has risen to 112/min and the 0650 hemoglobin has fallen to 10.4 g/dL.

c.text: (a) ‘preeclampsia with severe features’: Not a key. BP is normal. (b) ‘chorioamnionitis’: Not a key. Membranes are intact and she has no fever. (c) ‘preterm labor and birth’: Not a key. Possible, but contractions are mild and irregular. (d) ‘hemorrhagic shock’: Key. Ongoing bleeding from the placental site is the immediate threat.

e.text: (a) ‘mild irregular uterine tightening’: Not a key. Common with previa; not the main threat. (b) ‘smoking 5 cigarettes a day during pregnancy’: Not a key. A risk factor, not current evidence. (c) ‘ongoing bleeding, a rising HR and a falling Hgb’: Key. Bright red bleeding continues at 0700 (35 mL on the pad in 20 minutes), HR has risen from 84 to 108 to 112/min, and Hgb has fallen from 12.1 to 10.4 g/dL (0650 sample): blood loss is significant. (d) ‘a fetus in breech presentation at 33 weeks’: Not a key. Affects the birth plan, not immediate stability.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale (dyad) scoring: 1 point only when both the condition and its evidence are correct. A correct condition with the wrong evidence earns 0 of 1.
expanded.takeaway: Previa can bleed heavily without pain; measure loss and trend vital signs.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize by acuity. Trap: focusing on preterm birth before maternal bleeding.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0720 prescriptions. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: While resting in bed, the client should lie {{d1}}. The nurse should report {{d2}} to the HCP immediately. The nurse gives the betamethasone {{d3}}.

options.text: with the head lower than the hips
the client feeling the baby move
deep IM into a large muscle

rationale.short: Keep her on her side, report recurrent late decelerations at once, and give betamethasone deep IM. Supine and head-down positions, and IV, subcut or oral routes are wrong.

d1.text: (a) ‘on her side’: Key. A side-lying position keeps the uterus off the vena cava and improves blood flow to the placenta. (b) ‘with the head lower than the hips’: Not a key. Outdated Trendelenburg positioning. (c) ‘sitting upright at 90 degrees’: Not a key. Not needed; side-lying is preferred. (d) ‘flat on her back’: Not a key. Compresses the vena cava and lowers cardiac output.

d2.text: (a) ‘an FHR baseline of 145/min’: Not a key. Normal. (b) ‘the client feeling the baby move’: Not a key. Reassuring. (c) ‘recurrent late decelerations’: Key. A sign of fetal hypoxemia that may require birth. (d) ‘brown spotting on the pad’: Not a key. Old blood; document and continue to watch.

d3.text: (a) ‘by IV push over 1 minute’: Not a key. The suspension must not be given IV. (b) ‘subcutaneously in the abdomen’: Not a key. Wrong route. (c) ‘by mouth with water’: Not a key. The oral form is not used for fetal lung maturity. (d) ‘deep IM into a large muscle’: Key. Betamethasone suspension is for IM use only.

cases.title: ED trauma bay: driver after a highway crash

patient.history: Restrained driver in a highway crash at 1415; airbag deployed. No medical history. No medications. Tetanus up to date (booster 2 years ago).

entries.text: 1450: Arrived by ambulance. Airway patent, speaking full sentences. Breath sounds equal. Anxious and restless, GCS 15. Skin cool and pale; capillary refill 4 seconds. Seat-belt bruise across the lower chest and abdomen. Left upper abdominal tenderness. Reports left shoulder pain 6/10 with no shoulder injury found. Abrasion on the left forearm. Two 18-gauge IVs placed by EMS; 500 mL normal saline infused en route. FAST exam: free fluid in the left upper quadrant and pelvis.
1505: Massive transfusion protocol activated. Trauma surgeon at bedside: emergency laparotomy; OR notified and expecting the client. HCP prescriptions entered.

1640: Arrived in trauma ICU from the OR after laparotomy and splenectomy; bleeding controlled; extubated in the OR and awake. Received 4 units RBCs, 4 units plasma and 1 apheresis platelet unit through the warmer before and during surgery. TXA load complete; maintenance infusing. Client states his lips and fingertips 'feel tingly.' Warm blankets on; forced-air warmer running.

tabs.label: Intake and Output
rows: RBCs 2 units, plasma 2 units, platelets 1 unit

entries.text: 1505: Massive transfusion protocol (RBC:plasma:platelets 1:1:1) through rapid infuser/fluid warmer. Tranexamic acid 1 g in 100 mL normal saline IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g in 100 mL over 8 hours. Ionized calcium every 30 minutes during massive transfusion; calcium chloride per protocol. Forced-air warming. Fentanyl 25 mcg IV every 15 minutes PRN pain. Stop crystalloid.

a.text: Key. Poor peripheral perfusion.

rows.text: HR 128/min
Diastolic BP 88 mm Hg (pulse pressure 16 mm Hg)
Skin cool and pale
Lactate level of 3.8 mmol/L
Base excess -7 mEq/L
Left shoulder pain with no shoulder injury

rationale.short: Tachycardia, a raised diastolic BP and cool pale skin are sympathetic compensation. Lactate and the negative base excess show hypoperfusion. Left shoulder pain is referred from blood under the diaphragm.

r1.text: Sympathetic compensation (vasoconstriction, faster heart rate). Sympathetic response to keep cardiac output up.

r2.text: Sympathetic compensation (vasoconstriction, faster heart rate). Vasoconstriction raises diastolic pressure.

r3.text: Sympathetic compensation (vasoconstriction, faster heart rate). Sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood away from the skin to the vital organs.

r4.text: Cellular hypoperfusion (anaerobic metabolism). Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.

r5.text: Cellular hypoperfusion (anaerobic metabolism). Metabolic acidosis from poor perfusion (a base deficit of 7).

r6.text: Blood irritating the diaphragm. Referred pain (Kehr sign) from blood under the left diaphragm, often from the spleen.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{c}}, as shown by {{e1}} and {{e2}}.

options.text: cardiogenic shock from a cardiac contusion
a GCS score of 15 with anxiety
an SpO2 of 96% on room air
equal breath sounds on both sides
an abrasion on the left forearm
HR 128/min with a narrow pulse pressure

rationale.short: Hemorrhagic shock is most likely: a high lactate, plus tachycardia with a narrow pulse pressure. Neurogenic shock would cause bradycardia and warm skin.

c.text: (a) ‘hemorrhagic shock’: Key. Blunt injury, positive FAST and signs of poor perfusion. (b) ‘a panic reaction’: Not a key. Anxiety does not raise lactate or cause free fluid on FAST. (c) ‘cardiogenic shock from a cardiac contusion’: Not a key. No ECG changes or heart failure signs are described. (d) ‘neurogenic shock’: Not a key. Would cause warm skin and a slow heart rate.

e1.text: (a) ‘a lactate level of 3.8 mmol/L’: Key. Hypoperfusion; the base excess of -7 mEq/L agrees. (b) ‘a GCS score of 15 with anxiety’: Not a key. Alert; anxiety alone is not proof of shock. (c) ‘a hemoglobin level of 13.1 g/dL’: Not a key. Not yet changed. (d) ‘an SpO2 of 96% on room air’: Not a key. Adequate.

e2.text: (a) ‘equal breath sounds on both sides’: Not a key. Rules out a pneumothorax or hemothorax but is not evidence of shock. (b) ‘a temperature of 36.2 °C on arrival’: Not a key. Mildly low but not specific. (c) ‘an abrasion on the left forearm’: Not a key. Minor. (d) ‘HR 128/min with a narrow pulse pressure’: Key. Compensation for lost volume.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale (triad) scoring: if the condition (cause) is wrong the score is 0; otherwise 1 point for each correct piece of evidence. Maximum 2. Example: correct condition plus 1 correct effect earns 1 of 2.
expanded.takeaway: After blunt trauma, assume shock is from bleeding until proven otherwise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize the most likely life threat. Trap: attributing restlessness to anxiety.

options.text: Make sure 2 large-bore IV lines are working

f.text: Key. Hypothermia worsens bleeding (part of the 'lethal triad').

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1505 prescriptions. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The nurse sets the TXA loading dose to infuse at {{d1}}. TXA is given only when it can be started within {{d2}} of the injury. The nurse checks ionized calcium during the massive transfusion because {{d3}}.

options.text: a low body temperature makes the lab read falsely low
TXA binds calcium in the blood
the EMS saline diluted the calcium
citrate in stored blood binds calcium

rationale.short: The TXA load runs at 600 mL/h (100 mL over 10 minutes). TXA must start within 3 hours of injury, and ionized calcium is checked because citrate in stored blood binds it.

d1.text: (a) ‘10 mL/h’: Not a key. Far too slow. (b) ‘1,000 mL/h’: Not a key. Gives the dose in 6 minutes; rapid TXA can cause hypotension. (c) ‘600 mL/h’: Key. 100 mL over 10 minutes = 100 ÷ 10 × 60 = 600 mL/h. (d) ‘100 mL/h’: Not a key. That would take 1 hour.

d2.text: (a) ‘8 hours’: Not a key. That is how long the maintenance dose runs, not the start window. (b) ‘3 hours’: Key. Benefit is shown only when TXA starts within 3 hours; the crash was at 1415, so this order at 1505 qualifies. (c) ‘24 hours’: Not a key. Late TXA (after 3 hours) is not beneficial and may be harmful. (d) ‘1 hour’: Not a key. Earlier is better, but the window is 3 hours.

d3.text: (a) ‘a low body temperature makes the lab read falsely low’: Not a key. Hypothermia worsens bleeding, but it does not create a false low result. (b) ‘TXA binds calcium in the blood’: Not a key. TXA blocks fibrinolysis; it does not bind calcium. (c) ‘the EMS saline diluted the calcium’: Not a key. 500 mL of saline does not explain a low ionized calcium during massive transfusion. (d) ‘citrate in stored blood binds calcium’: Key. Each unit carries citrate anticoagulant, which binds ionized calcium and can cause tingling, weak contractions and bleeding.

cases.title: ED night shift: vomiting blood

patient.history: Alcohol-related cirrhosis; no alcohol for 8 months. Esophageal varices seen on endoscopy 1 year ago; prescribed propranolol 20 mg PO twice daily but has taken it 'off and on.' Takes ibuprofen 400 mg 2-3 times a week for back pain. Burning pain in the upper abdomen after meals for the past 2 weeks. No health insurance; works part-time as a cook.

entries.text: 2215: Brought by coworker. Vomited bright red blood twice at work, about 500 mL in total per coworker. One black, tarry stool tonight. Drowsy, opens eyes to voice, answers questions slowly but correctly. Spider angiomas on the chest. Palmar erythema. Abdomen mildly distended with shifting dullness. No asterixis. Two 18-gauge IVs placed.
2240: HCP at bedside; prescriptions entered. GI team aware; endoscopy planned.

Next day 0900: Endoscopy at 0130: 3 bands placed on bleeding esophageal varices. No further vomiting of blood. Received 2 units RBCs overnight. This morning says, 'I can't afford the propranolol, and I don't have a regular clinic.' Oriented to person and place but not date; flapping tremor of the hands noted at 0830.

2240: Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/h continuous infusion. Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours. NPO. Transfuse RBCs for hemoglobin below 7 g/dL. Hold propranolol. Endoscopy within 12 hours. Head of bed 30 degrees or higher; suction at bedside. Fresh frozen plasma 2 units for INR 1.8.

items.stem: Two sources could explain this upper GI bleed. For each finding, choose which source it points to.

columns.label: Points more to peptic ulcer bleeding

rows.text: Varices seen on endoscopy 1 year ago
Ibuprofen 2-3 times a week
Black, tarry stool
Shifting dullness and spider angiomas
Burning upper-abdominal pain after meals for 2 weeks
Taking propranolol 'off and on'

rationale.short: Known varices, signs of portal hypertension and missed propranolol point to varices. Ibuprofen use and burning pain after meals point to an ulcer. Melena fits either source.

r1.text: Points more to variceal bleeding. Known varices are the usual bleeding source in cirrhosis.

r2.text: Points more to peptic ulcer bleeding. NSAIDs damage the stomach and duodenal lining and cause ulcers.

r3.text: Fits either source equally. Any upper GI bleed causes melena.

r4.text: Points more to variceal bleeding. Ascites and spider angiomas are signs of cirrhosis with portal hypertension, the cause of varices.

r5.text: Points more to peptic ulcer bleeding. Dyspepsia-type pain is typical of a peptic ulcer; varices bleed without pain.

r6.text: Points more to variceal bleeding. Missed beta-blocker doses raise portal pressure.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client's shock index (HR ÷ SBP) is {{d1}}, which indicates {{d2}}. Because the client is drowsy and vomiting blood, the most immediate added risk is {{d3}}.

rationale.short: Shock index 122 ÷ 88 = 1.4 means significant blood loss. Drowsiness with vomiting adds a high risk of aspiration, so airway protection comes first.

d1.text: (a) ‘0.7’: Not a key. Normal range is about 0.5-0.7. (b) ‘0.4’: Not a key. Inverts the formula. (c) ‘2.2’: Not a key. Miscalculated. (d) ‘1.4’: Key. 122 ÷ 88 = 1.39, rounded to 1.4.

d2.text: (a) ‘fluid volume overload’: Not a key. The opposite problem. (b) ‘early septic shock’: Not a key. No infection signs. (c) ‘normal tissue perfusion’: Not a key. Not with 1.4. (d) ‘significant blood loss’: Key. A shock index of 1.0 or more suggests significant hypovolemia.

d3.text: (a) ‘a fall from the stretcher’: Not a key. A risk, but not the most immediate one. (b) ‘aspiration of blood’: Key. A drowsy client who is vomiting cannot protect the airway. (c) ‘alcohol withdrawal’: Not a key. Last drink was 8 months ago. (d) ‘hepatorenal syndrome’: Not a key. A later complication; creatinine is normal.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Bleeding plus drowsiness: protect the airway before anything else.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize with ABCs; calculation. Trap: going straight to fluids and ignoring the airway.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare to give an IV antibiotic
Prepare a balloon tamponade tube as the first treatment to stop the bleeding
Give lactulose 30 mL by mouth while he is actively vomiting blood
Make sure 2 large-bore IVs are working
Prepare to start an octreotide infusion
Lavage the stomach with iced saline to slow bleeding
Transfuse to keep the hemoglobin above 10 g/dL
Raise the head of the bed; keep suction ready

rationale.short: Protect the airway, keep NPO, secure IV access, and prepare octreotide and an IV antibiotic. High hemoglobin targets, oral lactulose during active vomiting, iced lavage and first-line balloon tamponade are wrong.

a.text: Key. Prophylactic antibiotics lower infection and death after a variceal bleed.

b.text: Key. Endoscopy is planned and the client is vomiting and drowsy.

c.text: Not a key. Balloon tamponade is a temporary rescue bridge for bleeding that cannot be controlled; first-line care is a vasoactive drug, antibiotics and endoscopy within 12 hours.

d.text: Not a key. Oral intake while vomiting and drowsy risks aspiration. Lactulose to prevent encephalopathy is reasonable once it can be given safely (by mouth, NG tube or enema).

e.text: Key. Needed for blood and drugs.

f.text: Key. Lowers portal pressure and bleeding.

g.text: Not a key. Outdated and harmful.

h.text: Not a key. High targets raise portal pressure and rebleeding; the threshold is about 7 g/dL.

rows.text: HR 92/min and BP 112/70 mm Hg
No further vomiting of blood after banding
Hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, then 8.5 g/dL on recheck (6.8 before 2 units)
Temperature 38.2 °C
Disoriented to date with a flapping tremor
'I can't afford the propranolol, and I don't have a regular clinic'

rationale.short: Vital signs, no further bleeding and a stable hemoglobin show improvement. A new fever and new encephalopathy need a report to the HCP. The cost and clinic barrier needs a social work referral.

r1.text: Shows improvement; continue the plan. Hemodynamics have recovered.

r2.text: Shows improvement; continue the plan. Bleeding controlled.

r3.text: Shows improvement; continue the plan. Rose as expected after 2 units and is stable on recheck: a change of 0.1 g/dL is within laboratory variation, so there is no sign of further bleeding.

r4.text: Report to the HCP. Possible infection, such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; report.

r5.text: Report to the HCP. New overt hepatic encephalopathy; report now and expect lactulose (also used to prevent encephalopathy after a variceal bleed).

r6.text: Refer to social work. A cost and access barrier: social work can find a clinic and a low-cost drug program so he keeps taking the beta-blocker that prevents rebleeding. The HCP can also be told, but the referral is the step that removes the barrier.

cases.title: ED: house-fire survivor

patient.history: Rescued from a bedroom fire at 0240 after about 10 minutes in a smoke-filled room. Preferred language Spanish; limited English. Asthma (albuterol PRN). Last tetanus shot unknown. Husband and 12-year-old son in the waiting room (uninjured).

entries.text: 0310: Video Spanish interpreter used. Partial- and full-thickness burns of the face, neck, chest (front and both sides; full thickness across the chest) and both arms (circumferential full-thickness burn of the right forearm); estimated 36% TBSA by Lund-Browder. Singed nasal hairs. Coughing black-flecked sputum. Voice hoarse; states, 'My head hurts and I feel confused.' Breath sounds with scattered wheezes. Pain 9/10. One 18-gauge IV in the left hand placed by EMS.

0335: Intubated (8.0 endotracheal tube) for progressing hoarseness and stridor. Two large-bore IVs placed. LR started per prescription. Indwelling urinary catheter placed. Husband asking for an update; son offers to interpret.

0830: Sedated, RASS -2. Ventilator peak airway pressure 38 cm H2O (was 26 at 0400). Full-thickness eschar across the front and sides of the chest now stiff and leathery; chest rise limited. Right hand cool, capillary refill 5 seconds; right radial pulse by Doppler only. Left hand warm, refill 2 seconds. LR at 340 mL/h.

0315: Oxygen 100% by nonrebreather. Prepare for intubation. Lactated Ringer's: initial rate per ABA formula 2 mL/kg/%TBSA over 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn; titrate hourly to urine output 30-50 mL/h. Morphine 4 mg IV every 1 hour PRN pain. Tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap) 0.5 mL IM. Tetanus immune globulin (TIG) 250 units IM at a separate site. Clean dry sheet over burns. Burn center transfer.

rows.text: Singed nasal hairs and burns of the face
Hoarse voice
Headache and confusion with SpO2 98% on room air
Carboxyhemoglobin 18%
Partial- and full-thickness burns over 36% TBSA
10 minutes in a smoke-filled room

rationale.short: Singed nasal hair with facial burns and hoarseness show airway injury; headache and confusion with a normal SpO2 and a COHb of 18% show CO poisoning; a 36% TBSA burn means burn shock. Enclosed-space exposure fits both.

r1.text: Inhalation (airway) injury. Heat reached the face and nose, so the upper airway may be burned and swelling.

r2.text: Inhalation (airway) injury. Swelling of the larynx; can progress to obstruction.

r3.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning. Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated, so SpO2 looks normal.

r4.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning. Confirms CO poisoning. A high COHb shows smoke exposure but does not by itself show airway injury, which is judged by airway signs (facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarseness) and bronchoscopy.

r5.text: Burn shock (fluid loss). Burns of 20% TBSA or more cause large capillary leaks.

r6.text: Inhalation (airway) injury + Carbon monoxide poisoning. Enclosed-space exposure raises the risk of both.
