items.stem: Is each statement about the client accurate or inaccurate?

rows.text: The SpO2 of 98% shows her oxygen delivery is adequate
Her hoarse voice means airway swelling may worsen over the next hours
Superficial burns are not counted in the TBSA used for fluids
A urine output of 60 mL/h would call for a faster LR rate
Fluids should be held until the airway is secured
The circumferential forearm burn needs regular pulse checks

rationale.short: SpO2 is falsely reassuring, fluids are not delayed, and a urine output above target calls for less fluid, not more. Hoarseness predicts worsening swelling, only partial- and full-thickness burns count toward TBSA, and circumferential burns need pulse checks.

r1.text: Inaccurate. CO-bound hemoglobin reads as normal on standard pulse oximetry.

r2.text: Accurate. Edema increases with fluid resuscitation.

r3.text: Accurate. Only partial- and full-thickness burns count.

r4.text: Inaccurate. 60 mL/h is above the 30-50 mL/h target (0.5 mL/kg/h for 68 kg is 34 mL/h); the LR rate would be lowered to avoid over-resuscitation.

r5.text: Inaccurate. Both start right away; fluids are not delayed.

r6.text: Accurate. Tight eschar can cut off blood flow.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0315 prescriptions. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The first priority is {{d1}} because {{d2}}. Using the prescribed formula, the estimated lactated Ringer's volume for the first 24 hours is {{d3}}.

options.text: hoarseness and sooty sputum mean airway swelling
her SpO2 of 98% shows she is not getting enough oxygen
a carboxyhemoglobin of 18% requires an endotracheal tube to treat
her wheezes show asthma that will not respond to albuterol

rationale.short: The airway comes first because hoarseness and soot signal swelling. The prescribed 24-hour estimate is 2 × 68 × 36 = 4,896 mL, half in the first 8 hours; 9,792 mL uses the old 4 mL formula.

d1.text: (a) ‘covering the burns with dressings’: Not a key. Later. (b) ‘starting IV fluids’: Not a key. Important, but the airway comes first. (c) ‘securing the airway’: Key. Hoarseness and soot signal swelling that can close the airway. (d) ‘treating her pain of 9/10’: Not a key. Important, after airway and breathing.

d2.text: (a) ‘hoarseness and sooty sputum mean airway swelling’: Key. Airway edema can block the airway within hours. (b) ‘her SpO2 of 98% shows she is not getting enough oxygen’: Not a key. SpO2 is falsely normal with CO poisoning, and 98% is not a reason to intubate. (c) ‘a carboxyhemoglobin of 18% requires an endotracheal tube to treat’: Not a key. 100% oxygen by nonrebreather treats CO. (Burn centers may also consider hydroxocobalamin when cyanide toxicity is suspected after an enclosed-space fire.) (d) ‘her wheezes show asthma that will not respond to albuterol’: Not a key. Wheezes after smoke inhalation do not mean albuterol has failed; the threat is upper-airway swelling.

d3.text: (a) ‘2,448 mL’: Not a key. This is only the first-8-hour half. (b) ‘9,792 mL’: Not a key. Uses 4 mL/kg (Parkland), not the prescribed 2 mL/kg. (c) ‘4,896 mL’: Key. 2 mL × 68 kg × 36% = 4,896 mL; half in the first 8 hours. (d) ‘1,360 mL’: Not a key. Uses 20% instead of 36% TBSA, and 1 mL/kg.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).

expanded.takeaway: The formula is a starting point; urine output drives the rate.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA/PHA: prioritize and calculate. Trap: using the 4 mL Parkland number by habit.

items.stem: The client is intubated and LR is running. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adjust the LR rate each hour based on urine output
Run LR at 1,000 mL/h until her BP rises
Give IV opioid doses for pain as prescribed
Use a qualified medical interpreter to update the husband
Give furosemide if urine output drops
Give Tdap and tetanus immune globulin as prescribed
Ask the 12-year-old son to interpret the update for his father

rationale.short: Titrate LR to urine output, give Tdap with TIG, use IV opioids and a qualified interpreter. A child interpreter, 1,000 mL/h and furosemide are wrong.

a.text: Key. Urine output (30-50 mL/h) guides the rate, not the formula.

b.text: Not a key. Over-resuscitation ('fluid creep') causes compartment syndromes and airway edema.

c.text: Key. IV route works reliably.

d.text: Key. Family communication needs a trained interpreter, not a child.

e.text: Not a key. Low urine output in burn shock is treated with more fluid, not diuretics.

f.text: Key. Her tetanus history is unknown and burns are tetanus-prone wounds, so CDC advises both vaccine and TIG 250 units.

g.text: Not a key. Minors should not interpret medical information.

cases.title: Stroke unit: BP after tenecteplase

patient.allergies: Angioedema with lisinopril (no other drug allergies)
patient.history: Acute ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery). Last known well 1215. Tenecteplase IV bolus (0.25 mg/kg, dose prepared by pharmacy) given at 1310. Hypertension; home medication amlodipine 10 mg daily (last dose this morning). No anticoagulants. Right-handed.

entries.text: 1320: NIHSS 9 (right arm drift, right facial droop, mild aphasia). BP 178/96 mm Hg before tenecteplase; 168/90 at 1330. Swallowed her morning pills without difficulty before the stroke. Bedside swallow screen not yet done.

1445: Neuro check (last one documented at 1400). NIHSS 9, unchanged. New headache since 1430: states, 'My head hurts,' rated 4/10. No nausea. No new weakness. IV site in left forearm: no bleeding. No gum or urine bleeding. Spouse asks if she can give her the aspirin from home now.
1450: HCP notified at 1447 of the 1445 BP and the new headache. BP protocol started. HCP prescribed a stat noncontrast head CT.

1452 and 1505: labetalol 10 mg IV given per protocol (BP and HR rechecks in Vital Signs). 1520: head CT read as no hemorrhage; HCP aware. Neuro checks every 15 minutes to 1510, then every 30 minutes: NIHSS 9 through 1730. Headache 4/10 to 1730.

1800: NIHSS 11 (new right leg weakness). Headache now 7/10 and vomited once. Swallow screen not yet done. Spouse has put a bottle of aspirin tablets on the bedside table and says she will give one 'to thin the blood'.

Neuro checks and BP: every 15 minutes x 2 hours, every 30 minutes x 6 hours, then hourly x 16 hours after thrombolysis. Notify HCP at once for new or worsening headache, nausea, vomiting or any worsening neuro exam. NPO until swallow screen passed. No antiplatelet or anticoagulant for 24 hours after tenecteplase. Repeat head CT at 24 hours (about 1310 tomorrow). After that CT shows no hemorrhage and a swallow screen is passed: aspirin 325 mg PO once, then 81 mg PO daily. Hold home amlodipine while NPO.

Post-thrombolysis BP protocol (standing order): for BP at or above 180/105 mm Hg, give labetalol 10 mg IV over 1-2 minutes; may repeat every 10-20 minutes, up to 3 doses. Recheck BP and HR 5 minutes after each dose. Hold for HR below 60/min. Target: BP below 180/105 mm Hg. Notify HCP when the protocol is started and if BP is still at or above 180/105 after 3 doses.
1450: Stat noncontrast head CT for new headache after thrombolysis. Continue post-thrombolysis BP protocol.

rationale.short: High BP, a new headache and recent tenecteplase relate to bleeding. No swallow screen and facial droop relate to aspiration. Oral aspirin relates to both.

r1.text: Intracranial hemorrhage. High BP raises bleeding risk after thrombolysis.

r2.text: Intracranial hemorrhage. A new headache after thrombolysis can be the first sign of bleeding into the brain.

r3.text: Intracranial hemorrhage. A thrombolytic dissolves clots everywhere, so bleeding risk is highest in the first 24 hours.

r4.text: Aspiration. Stroke commonly impairs swallowing; nothing by mouth until a screen is passed.

r5.text: Both risks. Antiplatelets are held for 24 hours after thrombolysis (bleeding), and a pill by mouth before a swallow screen risks aspiration.

r6.text: Aspiration. Facial and tongue weakness impair the swallow.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: For the next 24 hours the BP target is {{d1}}. The nurse should {{d2}} because {{d3}}.

options.text: start the IV labetalol BP protocol
give nothing and recheck the BP in 1 hour
give her home amlodipine by mouth
start a nitroprusside infusion right away
her brain needs a BP above 180/105 to stay perfused
high BP raises her risk of brain bleeding
her glucose is above the 140 mg/dL mark

rationale.short: The 24-hour target is below 180/105, so start the IV labetalol protocol. Driving BP below 140 is not recommended, and oral amlodipine is too slow and she is NPO.

d1.text: (a) ‘below 140/90 mm Hg’: Not a key. Intensive lowering after thrombolysis is not recommended. (b) ‘below 120/80 mm Hg’: Not a key. Too low; can worsen the stroke. (c) ‘below 185/110 mm Hg’: Not a key. That is the target before giving thrombolysis. (d) ‘below 180/105 mm Hg’: Key. The post-thrombolysis target.

d2.text: (a) ‘start the IV labetalol BP protocol’: Key. The BP is above 180/105, and the standing protocol covers it. (b) ‘give nothing and recheck the BP in 1 hour’: Not a key. Delays treatment of a high BP. (c) ‘give her home amlodipine by mouth’: Not a key. She is NPO, and an oral drug acts too slowly to bring BP under 180/105. (d) ‘start a nitroprusside infusion right away’: Not a key. Reserved for refractory BP; not first-line.

d3.text: (a) ‘her HR has risen above 80/min’: Not a key. Not a reason to treat BP. (b) ‘her brain needs a BP above 180/105 to stay perfused’: Not a key. After thrombolysis the target is below 180/105; higher pressure raises bleeding risk. (c) ‘high BP raises her risk of brain bleeding’: Key. The reason for the target: above 180/105 the risk climbs. (d) ‘her glucose is above the 140 mg/dL mark’: Not a key. 142 is within the 140-180 target.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Know both numbers: 185/110 before thrombolysis, 180/105 for 24 hours after.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize the right target. Trap: 'lower is better' after a stroke.

items.stem: Select the 3 actions the nurse should plan to take now.

options.text: Start the BP protocol and report the headache to the HCP
Explain to the spouse why aspirin is held for now
Start an insulin infusion now for the glucose of 142 mg/dL
Give the aspirin 81 mg by mouth now as the spouse asks
Lower the head of the bed flat
Keep the client NPO until a swallow screen is passed

rationale.short: Start the BP protocol and notify the HCP, keep her NPO and explain why aspirin is held. Giving aspirin, lying flat, an insulin infusion for 142 and Trendelenburg are wrong.

a.text: Key. The protocol covers the BP; a new headache after thrombolysis needs the HCP at once.

b.text: Key. Antiplatelets raise bleeding risk right after thrombolysis.

c.text: Not a key. The stroke target is 140-180; tight control is not recommended.

d.text: Not a key. Contraindicated for 24 hours and she is NPO.

e.text: Not a key. Head of bed 30 degrees is used unless otherwise prescribed.

f.text: Key. Prevents aspiration.

g.text: Not a key. Outdated and unsafe.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 3 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 3 choices. Maximum 3. Example: choosing 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Nothing by mouth and no antiplatelets for 24 hours after thrombolysis.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan SAF/PA: plan post-thrombolysis safety. Trap: treating a glucose of 142 aggressively.

items.stem: At 1450 the nurse starts the post-thrombolysis BP protocol. Is each action indicated or contraindicated?

rows.text: Give labetalol 10 mg IV over 1-2 minutes
Recheck BP and HR 5 minutes after the dose
Hold the dose if HR is below 60/min
Repeat the dose 2 minutes after the first if the BP is still 180/105 or higher
Push the labetalol as fast as possible
Keep giving doses until SBP is below 140 mm Hg

rationale.short: Give labetalol 10 mg IV over 1-2 minutes, recheck BP and HR, and hold if HR is below 60. Repeating the dose after 2 minutes, rapid push and targeting SBP below 140 are contraindicated.

r1.text: Indicated. First-line IV agent for post-thrombolysis BP.

r2.text: Indicated. Labetalol lowers HR as well as BP.

r3.text: Indicated. Avoids symptomatic bradycardia.

r4.text: Contraindicated. The protocol spaces doses 10-20 minutes apart, with a BP and HR recheck 5 minutes after each dose; stacking doses risks hypotension and bradycardia.

r5.text: Contraindicated. Rapid push can cause severe hypotension and bradycardia.

r6.text: Contraindicated. Intensive lowering below 140 after thrombolysis is not recommended.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Give the IV dose slowly, recheck, and stop at the target.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PHA: administer antihypertensives safely. Trap: pushing too fast or too far.

rnFlags: PharmD check: post-thrombolysis labetalol protocol as written (10 mg IV over 1-2 min, repeat every 10-20 min up to 3 doses, hold HR <60, notify after 3 doses). Confirm the facility escalation step (e.g., nicardipine infusion) is acceptable to leave out of the item. v3 removed the sublingual nifedipine row (not guideline-appropriate for acute BP lowering).

PharmD check: aspirin order rewritten to start after the 24-hour post-tenecteplase CT (about 1310 next day) and a passed swallow screen: aspirin 325 mg PO once, then 81 mg daily (AHA/ASA: antiplatelets withheld 24 h after IVT; aspirin within 48 h of onset; 160-325 mg initial dose). Confirm dose and route (rectal if swallow screen failed).

PharmD check: tenecteplase is described as 0.25 mg/kg prepared by pharmacy (64 kg = 16 mg by guideline math; FDA AIS label weight tier 60-<70 kg = 17.5 mg). No item keys on the number; confirm which the facility dispenses.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1800 findings. For each finding, specify whether it is acceptable or needs action now.

rows.text: BP 152/86 mm Hg
HR 78/min
Glucose 156 mg/dL
Headache 7/10 with one episode of vomiting
NIHSS 11 (was 9)
Aspirin tablets at the bedside, spouse plans to give one

rationale.short: BP, HR and glucose are acceptable. A worsening headache with vomiting, a rising NIHSS and the spouse's plan to give aspirin each need action now.

r1.text: Acceptable now. Below 180/105 and falling steadily; no BP action is needed at this moment.

r2.text: Acceptable now. Above the hold threshold.

r3.text: Acceptable now. Within the 140-180 target.

r4.text: Needs action now. Worsening headache and vomiting suggest intracranial bleeding; call the HCP now and expect a stat CT.

r5.text: Needs action now. New deficits; report now.

r6.text: Needs action now. Remove the aspirin and teach now: antiplatelets are held for 24 hours, and bleeding is now suspected.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Evaluate outcomes: compare new data with the earlier timepoint; decide what improved, what did not and what needs action now.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: A BP at goal does not mean the client is safe; recheck the neuro exam (and, with her ACE-inhibitor angioedema history, the lips and tongue for orolingual angioedema after thrombolysis).
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: evaluate for hemorrhagic conversion. Trap: stopping at the BP number.

cases.title: Ortho unit: 'He's not making sense'

patient.history: Left hip hemiarthroplasty yesterday under spinal anesthesia for a fall-related hip fracture. Atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily at home (last dose 3 days ago; held before surgery). Since surgery: enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily for VTE prophylaxis; surgeon plans to restart apixaban on day 2 or 3 after surgery. Hypertension. Retired machinist; lives with his wife. Right-handed. Full code.

entries.text: 0500 (night RN): Slept well. Oriented x 4. Speech clear. Moving all extremities; left leg limited by surgery. 0800: Alert, oriented, joking with the nurse during morning medications. Ate 50% of breakfast.

0915: AP reports the client 'isn't making sense.' Client awake, trying to speak but cannot find words; speech slurred. Right side of the face droops. Right arm drifts down within 5 seconds. Eyes look to the left. Follows simple commands; keeps eye contact and stays focused on the nurse throughout the exam. Left hip dressing dry. Pain 3/10 by pointing to the scale.
0920: Nurse checked POC glucose: 118 mg/dL. 0930: Stroke team at bedside. NIHSS 12. CT and CT angiography ordered. Current IV: 22-gauge in the back of the right hand.

1330: CT angiography at 0950 showed a left middle cerebral artery occlusion; stroke team chose thrombectomy without thrombolysis (major surgery yesterday). Returned from mechanical thrombectomy (artery opened) at 1215. Right femoral sheath removed; site soft, no hematoma; right pedal pulses 2+, the same as before the procedure. Speaking in full sentences; names objects correctly. Right arm holds up for 10 seconds without drift. NIHSS 2. Groin pain 2/10. Urine output 60 mL/h.

tabs.label: MAR
rows: Restart day 2-3 after surgery per surgeon
Oxycodone 5 mg PO every 4 h PRN pain

options.text: Right arm drifts down within 5 seconds
Left hip dressing dry and intact

b.text: Not a key. Normal.

c.text: Key. New language and speech deficit.

d.text: Not a key. Expected.

items.stem: For each finding or risk factor, specify whether it fits an acute stroke, delirium, or both.

rows.text: Right facial droop and right arm drift
Eyes look to the left
Atrial fibrillation with apixaban stopped 3 days ago
Oxycodone at 0600 on the first day after surgery
Change from normal at 0800
Cannot find words, yet follows commands and stays focused on the nurse

rationale.short: Facial droop, arm drift, gaze deviation, aphasia and AF off full anticoagulation point to stroke. An opioid on the first day after surgery is a delirium risk. An acute change fits both.

r1.text: Acute stroke. One-sided weakness is focal; delirium does not cause it.

r2.text: Acute stroke. Gaze deviation is a focal sign.

r3.text: Acute stroke. Time off full anticoagulation raises AF-related embolic stroke risk.

r4.text: Delirium. Opioids and recent surgery are classic delirium risk factors.

r5.text: Both. Both cause an acute change.

r6.text: Acute stroke. Aphasia with intact attention is a focal cortical sign. Delirium can disorder speech, but its core feature is inattention, which is absent here.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Focal signs separate stroke from delirium.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: analyze neurologic cues in older adults. Trap: diagnostic overshadowing by age and surgery.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client's last known well time is {{d1}}. Before treatment decisions, the team must rule out {{d2}}, and this check is needed {{d3}}.

options.text: the time the CT is done
when the client has a known history of diabetes
after the CT scan has been read
when the client is also drowsy or sweaty
for any client with suspected stroke signs

rationale.short: Last known well is 0800, the last time he was seen normal. Hypoglycemia must be ruled out with a bedside glucose in every suspected stroke before treatment decisions.

d1.text: (a) ‘the time the CT is done’: Not a key. Not related to symptom onset. (b) ‘0915’: Not a key. That is when the deficits were found, not when he was last normal. (c) ‘0500’: Not a key. He was seen normal later, at 0800. (d) ‘0800’: Key. He was last seen normal at the 0800 medication pass.

d2.text: (a) ‘a urinary tract infection’: Not a key. Can worsen confusion but does not cause focal signs. (b) ‘hypoglycemia’: Key. Low glucose can mimic a stroke and is quickly treatable. (c) ‘constipation’: Not a key. Not a stroke mimic. (d) ‘hyperkalemia’: Not a key. Does not cause focal deficits.

d3.text: (a) ‘when the client has a known history of diabetes’: Not a key. Low glucose can occur without diabetes (e.g., poor intake after surgery). (b) ‘after the CT scan has been read’: Not a key. It is checked at once; it should not wait for imaging. (c) ‘when the client is also drowsy or sweaty’: Not a key. Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke without these signs, so glucose is checked in every suspected stroke. (d) ‘for any client with suspected stroke signs’: Key. Glucose is the one test required before reperfusion decisions in all clients, with or without diabetes.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Last known well is the last time seen normal, not the time symptoms were found.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC/PA: prioritize time-critical information. Trap: using the discovery time.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take now? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop neuro checks until the stroke team arrives
Report the last known well time
Report the surgery yesterday and the anticoagulant doses
Give aspirin 325 mg by mouth now to keep the clot from growing
Keep the client NPO until a swallow screen
Give the PRN oxycodone to calm him
Wait 30 minutes to see whether symptoms resolve

rationale.short: Activate the stroke alert, report last known well, the surgery and the anticoagulant doses, and keep him NPO. Sedation, waiting, aspirin and stopping neuro checks are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. Checks continue so changes are caught.

b.text: Key. Decides which treatments are still possible.

c.text: Key. Recent major surgery and anticoagulant timing decide thrombolysis eligibility and procedure planning.

d.text: Not a key. Not before imaging, and he is NPO.

e.text: Key. Prevents aspiration.

f.text: Not a key. Sedation masks the neuro exam.

g.text: Key. Brings the stroke team to the bedside.

h.text: Not a key. Delays time-critical treatment.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 4. Example: selecting 3 keys and 1 distractor earns 3 - 1 = 2 of 4.
expanded.takeaway: In-hospital stroke: call it, time it, list surgery and anticoagulants, nothing by mouth.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC: escalate in an emergency. Trap: 'wait and see' in a post-op client.

items.stem: At 0930 the stroke team orders CT and CT angiography. Select the 3 actions the nurse should take while the client waits for transport to CT.

options.text: Give labetalol to bring the BP below 140/90 before the CT
Place a 20-gauge or larger antecubital IV for the contrast
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter before the CT
Give the 1400 acetaminophen dose now by mouth for comfort
Wait for a repeat hemoglobin result before sending the client to CT
Go with the client to CT on a cardiac monitor
Recheck the neuro exam and BP at 15-minute intervals

rationale.short: Keep checking the neuro exam and BP, place an antecubital IV of 20 gauge or larger for the CT angiogram and go with him to CT on a monitor. Oral acetaminophen, lowering a BP that is already below 185/110, a urinary catheter and waiting for other labs are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. BP 176/94 is already below 185/110; lowering it further can reduce flow to the brain.

b.text: Key. CT angiography needs a large, proximal IV; the 22-gauge hand IV is too small for the contrast injection rate.

c.text: Not a key. Not needed now, delays imaging, and adds infection and bleeding risk.

d.text: Not a key. He is NPO until a swallow screen is passed.

e.text: Not a key. Only the glucose must be known before treatment decisions; other labs must not delay imaging.

f.text: Key. He has atrial fibrillation and an evolving stroke; a nurse who knows him stays with him during transport.

g.text: Key. Catches worsening deficits or BP above 185/110 before a treatment decision.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 3 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 3 choices. Maximum 3. Example: choosing 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: While waiting for imaging: keep watching, get the access the scan needs, and do not delay the scan.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan MOC/PA: carry out time-critical stroke care. Trap: lowering BP that is already in range, or letting routine tasks delay imaging.

cases.title: Rehab unit: sudden pounding headache

patient.history: T4 complete spinal cord injury 2 years ago. Neurogenic bladder managed with intermittent catheterization every 6 hours (0600, 1200, 1800, 0000). Neurogenic bowel program. Takes sildenafil 50 mg as needed for erectile function. Baseline BP 100/64 mm Hg. Full code.

entries.text: 1200: Intermittent catheterization due. Client in physical therapy until 1330; catheterization was not done. 1400: Returned from therapy. Denies headache. BP 102/66 mm Hg.

1540: Client reports a sudden pounding headache, 9/10, with blurred vision and nausea. Face, neck and shoulders flushed and sweaty. Skin below the nipple line (abdomen and legs) cool and pale, with goosebumps. Anxious, states, 'Something is very wrong.' Abdomen firm and distended. No urine output since 0600 (catheterization at 0600 drained 420 mL).
1555: Sitting upright with legs lowered. Clothing loosened. BP 184/102 mm Hg. States he took sildenafil at about 1130, before therapy. HCP notified; prescriptions entered.

1630: Catheterization at 1605 drained 650 mL clear urine. BP now 92/58 mm Hg; client dizzy when sitting up. Headache resolved. Face no longer flushed. Abdomen soft. Client asks, 'How do I stop this from happening again?'
Intermittent catheterization every 6 hours. Notify HCP for SBP 150 mm Hg or higher with symptoms. Autonomic dysreflexia protocol on chart.

1558: Captopril 25 mg sublingual now (client took sildenafil today). Lidocaine jelly 2% in urethra; wait about 5 minutes if possible, then catheterize. Check BP and HR every 1-2 minutes until stable, then every 2-5 minutes. Call HCP if SBP remains 150 mm Hg or higher after the bladder is emptied.

cases.revealRule: Chart content tagged with a time point is shown only when the student reaches an item at or after that time point; 'baseline' is shown from the start. Tables use rowTimepoints or columnTimepoints (the latest applicable tag wins).

items.stem: For each finding, specify what it best represents. Choose one column for each finding.

columns.label: Sign above the level of injury
Sign below the level of injury

rows.text: Face, neck and shoulders flushed and sweaty
Pounding headache with blurred vision
Skin of the abdomen and legs cool and pale
Goosebumps on the abdomen and legs
Abdomen firm and distended
No urine output since 0600

rationale.short: Flushing and the headache are above the injury; cool pale skin and goosebumps are below it. A distended abdomen and no urine since 0600 point to the trigger.

r1.text: Sign above the level of injury. Vasodilation above the lesion.

r2.text: Sign above the level of injury. From the sudden BP rise, sensed above the lesion.

r3.text: Sign below the level of injury. Sympathetic vasoconstriction below a T4 lesion.

r4.text: Sign below the level of injury. Sympathetic piloerection below the lesion.

r5.text: Clue to the trigger. Points to a full bladder, the most common trigger.

r6.text: Clue to the trigger. The 1200 catheterization was missed.

expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Above the lesion: red and sweaty. Below: pale, cool, goosebumps. Then find the trigger.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: recognize autonomic dysreflexia. Trap: treating it as a simple headache.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1540 findings. For each finding, specify whether it is expected after a T4 complete injury or is a new finding that needs explanation.

columns.label: Expected after a T4 complete injury

rows.text: Neurogenic bladder with intermittent catheterization
BP 102/66 mm Hg at 1400 (baseline 100/64)
SBP 178 mm Hg at 1540
HR 52/min (72/min at 1400)
Pounding headache rated 9/10
Face flushed and sweaty; skin below the nipple line pale

rationale.short: A neurogenic bladder and a low baseline BP are expected after a T4 injury. A sudden SBP of 178, a slow heart rate, a severe headache and the flush-and-pale pattern are new and need a cause.

r1.text: Expected after a T4 complete injury. Expected below a T4 lesion.

r2.text: Expected after a T4 complete injury. Near his usual BP; a lower baseline BP is common after SCI.

r3.text: New finding needing explanation. Far above his own baseline; needs a cause.

r4.text: New finding needing explanation. His own rate was 72 at 1400; a sudden slow rate with a high BP is a baroreceptor response that needs a cause.

r5.text: New finding needing explanation. New and severe.

r6.text: New finding needing explanation. A new above-and-below pattern.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 6. Example: one wrong row earns 5 of 6.
expanded.takeaway: Compare the BP with the client's own baseline, not with 120/80.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: separate expected SCI findings from new ones. Trap: calling everything expected.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{c}} triggered by {{e1}} and shown by {{e2}}.

options.text: a full bladder from a missed catheter time
a bowel impaction from a missed bowel program
tight clothing or a leg-bag strap on the thigh
a pressure injury on the sacrum
an SpO2 of 97% on room air
a BP of 102/66 mm Hg at 1400
an SBP of 178 and an HR of 52/min

rationale.short: Autonomic dysreflexia from a full bladder, shown by SBP 178 with HR 52. A migraine does not cause this BP and heart rate pattern.

c.text: (a) ‘autonomic dysreflexia’: Key. The BP, bradycardia and flush/pale pattern in a T4 injury. (b) ‘a migraine with aura’: Not a key. Migraine does not raise SBP by 76 mm Hg with bradycardia. (c) ‘malignant hyperthermia’: Not a key. Not exposed to anesthetic agents; no fever or rigidity. (d) ‘early sepsis from a UTI’: Not a key. No fever, and the pattern is not infectious.

e1.text: (a) ‘a full bladder from a missed catheter time’: Key. The most common trigger, and it fits the timeline. (b) ‘a bowel impaction from a missed bowel program’: Not a key. Possible in general, but there is direct evidence for the bladder. (c) ‘tight clothing or a leg-bag strap on the thigh’: Not a key. Not described. (d) ‘a pressure injury on the sacrum’: Not a key. None is described.

e2.text: (a) ‘an SpO2 of 97% on room air’: Not a key. Normal. (b) ‘a BP of 102/66 mm Hg at 1400’: Not a key. Near his baseline of 100/64; it does not show AD. (c) ‘an SBP of 178 and an HR of 52/min’: Key. The defining cardiovascular response. (d) ‘a temperature of 36.9 °C’: Not a key. Normal; not a sign of AD.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale (triad) scoring: if the condition (cause) is wrong the score is 0; otherwise 1 point for each correct piece of evidence. Maximum 2. Example: correct condition plus 1 correct effect earns 1 of 2.
expanded.takeaway: In a client with SCI at T6 or above, this pattern is AD until proven otherwise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize the emergency. Trap: treating the headache as primary.

items.stem: Select the 3 actions the nurse should plan to take first.

options.text: Loosen clothing and check for other triggers
Sit the client upright and lower the legs
Give acetaminophen and recheck in 30 minutes
Lay the client flat and raise the legs
Start a digital rectal exam now

rationale.short: Sit him up, loosen clothing and check BP every 1-2 minutes. Lying flat, waiting on acetaminophen, a rectal exam first and oral fluids are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. Does not treat AD and risks aspiration if nauseated.

b.text: Key. Removes simple causes fast.

c.text: Key. Lowers BP immediately by pooling blood in the legs.

d.text: Not a key. Delays treatment of a hypertensive emergency.

e.text: Key. AD can swing quickly.

f.text: Not a key. The opposite of what lowers BP.

g.text: Not a key. Bowel checks come after the bladder, and only after BP medicine if SBP is 150 or higher.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1558 prescriptions and the client's statement about sildenafil. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lay the client flat after the medication
Press firmly on the lower abdomen to empty the bladder
Use lidocaine jelly and wait about 5 minutes before catheterizing
Irrigate the bladder with 60 mL of cold saline before draining it
Avoid nitrates; sildenafil was taken in the last 24 hours
Apply nitroglycerin paste to the chest
Give captopril 25 mg sublingual as prescribed

rationale.short: Avoid nitrates after sildenafil, give captopril SL, and use lidocaine jelly and wait. Nitro paste, cold irrigation, Credé and lying flat are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. Keep him sitting up while BP is high.

b.text: Not a key. Credé maneuver is contraindicated.

c.text: Key. Reduces the stimulus of catheterization; PVA 2020 Rec 2.15: wait approximately 5 minutes, if possible.

d.text: Not a key. Cold fluid triggers more AD; use 10-15 mL of body-temperature fluid.

e.text: Key. Nitrates with a PDE5 inhibitor can cause severe, prolonged hypotension.

f.text: Not a key. Contraindicated: PVA 2020 says not to use nitropaste within 24 hours of sildenafil (severe hypotension).

g.text: Key. PVA 2020 names captopril 25 mg sublingual once for AD when nitrates are contraindicated (note to Rec 3.6; Appendix 2): onset within 15 minutes, short acting, and safe after sildenafil.

cases.title: Medical unit: weaker every hour

patient.history: Diarrheal illness (Campylobacter) 3 weeks ago. Admitted 3 days ago with ascending leg weakness and tingling; diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome. IV immune globulin (IVIG) started 2 days ago; today's dose is day 3 of 5. No other conditions. Full code.

entries.text: Day 3 2000: Legs 2/5 strength, arms 4/5. Reflexes absent in legs. Voice normal. Ate dinner without coughing. Single-breath count 22.

0800: Voice softer; speaks 4-5 words per breath. Single-breath count 14. Cough weak. Coughed and sputtered while drinking water at 0730. Legs 2/5, unchanged; arms 3/5. Reflexes absent. Tingling in both feet. Low back pain 4/10. Pulse oximeter HR readings swing between 58 and 128/min over the past hour. Skin warm and dry.
0820: HCP notified with VC trend; prescriptions entered (see Orders).

1100: In ICU. Breathing rapid and shallow; abdomen moves inward with each breath in. Using neck muscles to breathe. Single-breath count 8. Anxious. Skin warm and pink; no cyanosis. Anesthesia team called to bedside.
Vital capacity and NIF every 6 hours. IVIG 0.4 g/kg IV daily x 5 days. Enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily. Lorazepam 0.5 mg IV every 6 hours PRN anxiety. Regular diet. Physical therapy.

0820: Transfer to ICU now. Vital capacity and NIF every 2 hours. NPO pending speech-language pathology swallow evaluation. Continuous cardiac monitoring. Continue IVIG. Bag-valve mask and suction at bedside.

items.stem: For each finding, specify the complication or complications it puts the client at risk for. Each finding may fit more than one column.

rows.text: Falling vital capacity
Single-breath count 14
Weak cough
Coughing and sputtering while drinking water
HR 58-128/min swings
BP 168/96 then 98/60 mm Hg within an hour

rationale.short: Low VC, a falling breath count and a weak cough mean respiratory failure risk; a weak cough and coughing on water mean aspiration risk (the weak cough belongs in both columns); HR and BP swings mean autonomic crisis risk.

r1.text: Respiratory failure (weak breathing muscles). Weak diaphragm.

r2.text: Respiratory failure (weak breathing muscles). Weak breathing muscles.

r3.text: Respiratory failure (weak breathing muscles) + Aspiration (weak swallowing and airway protection). Both columns are correct, and each earns a point. A weak cough comes from weak expiratory (breathing) muscles, a sign of respiratory failure risk, and a weak cough cannot clear food, fluid or secretions from the airway, a sign of aspiration risk.

r4.text: Aspiration (weak swallowing and airway protection). Bulbar (swallowing) weakness lets water enter the airway.

r5.text: Autonomic crisis. Dysautonomia.

r6.text: Autonomic crisis. Labile BP from dysautonomia.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring within each column: +1 for each correct check, -1 for each incorrect check, each column floored at 0. Maximum 7. Example: one extra wrong check in a column cancels one correct check in that column.
expanded.takeaway: GBS kills through breathing, swallowing and the autonomic system.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: link cues to complications. Trap: treating the BP numbers alone.

items.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client's vital capacity is about {{d1}} mL/kg. This indicates {{d2}}, so the nurse should {{d3}}.

options.text: encourage incentive spirometry and recheck later today
give the PRN lorazepam to calm his anxiety
notify the HCP to evaluate for ICU transfer
recheck the vital capacity in 6 hours when the infusion ends

rationale.short: 1,620 ÷ 90 = 18 mL/kg, below 20 mL/kg and falling: impending respiratory failure. Notify the HCP for ICU evaluation now.

d1.text: (a) ‘1.8’: Not a key. Decimal error. (b) ‘18’: Key. 1,620 mL ÷ 90 kg = 18 mL/kg. (c) ‘24’: Not a key. Miscalculated. (d) ‘30’: Not a key. That was the admission value (2,700 ÷ 90).

d2.text: (a) ‘impending respiratory failure’: Key. Below 20 mL/kg and falling fast. (b) ‘normal breathing reserve’: Not a key. Reserve is low. (c) ‘early aspiration pneumonia’: Not a key. No fever or crackles. (d) ‘anxiety-related breathing’: Not a key. The numbers are objective muscle weakness.

d3.text: (a) ‘encourage incentive spirometry and recheck later today’: Not a key. Does not treat muscle failure and delays escalation. (b) ‘give the PRN lorazepam to calm his anxiety’: Not a key. Sedation can stop breathing. (c) ‘notify the HCP to evaluate for ICU transfer’: Key. Needs close monitoring and possible intubation. (d) ‘recheck the vital capacity in 6 hours when the infusion ends’: Not a key. Too long; it is falling quickly.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: In GBS, a VC near 20 mL/kg means call now; do not wait for the SpO2 to drop.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: calculate and escalate. Trap: waiting for the next scheduled check.

r6.text: Not indicated. He cannot bear weight safely; clots are prevented with enoxaparin and devices.

items.stem: Two hours after ICU transfer, the nurse evaluates the client's breathing at 1100. For each finding, choose the one column that best describes what it shows.

rows.text: Vital capacity 1,350 mL (15 mL/kg), down from 1,620 mL at 0800
NIF -18 cm H2O, down from -28
Abdomen moves inward with each breath in
PaCO2 48 mm Hg
SpO2 95% on 2 L/min
Skin warm and pink; no cyanosis

rationale.short: A falling VC and NIF and paradoxical breathing show breathing-muscle strength is still falling. A PaCO2 of 48 with a pH of 7.32 shows CO2 is building up. SpO2 95% on oxygen and pink skin are falsely reassuring.

r1.text: Breathing-muscle strength is still falling. Below the 20 mL/kg warning level and still falling despite ICU care.

r2.text: Breathing-muscle strength is still falling. Weaker than -30 cm H2O; the diaphragm cannot generate force.

r3.text: Breathing-muscle strength is still falling. Paradoxical breathing: the diaphragm is failing.

r4.text: CO2 is building up. Above 45 mm Hg: the weak muscles can no longer clear CO2.

r5.text: CO2 is building up. With the high PaCO2, this is acute respiratory acidosis.

r6.text: Looks reassuring but is not. Oxygen keeps the saturation up while ventilation fails; CO2 is already rising.

r7.text: Looks reassuring but is not. Cyanosis is a late sign; its absence does not mean ventilation is adequate.

expanded.takeaway: Rising CO2 with a normal SpO2 on oxygen = time to intubate.

cases.title: PACU: fever and racing heart after an appendectomy

patient.history: Graves disease; stopped methimazole 3 months ago when she lost her insurance. Laparoscopic appendectomy this morning for uncomplicated appendicitis under general anesthesia (sevoflurane, rocuronium). Latex-safe room. Full code.

entries.text: 1130: Arrived in PACU, extubated. Drowsy, arousable. Pain 5/10. HR 104/min. Incisions dry.

1230: Agitated, pulling at blankets; oriented to person, not place or time. Skin hot, flushed and sweaty. Fine tremor of the hands. Jaw relaxed, muscles not rigid. Loose stool x 1. Lungs clear. Incisions dry. Pain 3/10. EtCO2 by nasal cannula 36 mm Hg. Monitor: irregular narrow-complex rhythm, 156/min.
1245: Anesthesia and HCP at bedside; prescriptions entered (see Orders).
1630: In ICU. Calmer, oriented x 3. Monitor: sinus rhythm 104/min. Fine crackles at both lung bases; SpO2 91% on 4 L/min (was 96% on 2 L). Feet with mild edema.

1245: Propranolol 60 mg PO (or via NG tube if unable to swallow safely) now, then every 4 hours (hold for SBP below 100 mm Hg or HR below 60/min). Propylthiouracil 500 mg PO now, then 250 mg every 4 hours. Potassium iodide (SSKI) 5 drops PO every 6 hours, first dose 1 hour after PTU. Hydrocortisone 300 mg IV now, then 100 mg every 8 hours. Acetaminophen 1,000 mg PO now. Cooling blanket. Transfer to ICU.

items.stem: The anesthesia provider asks if this could be malignant hyperthermia from the anesthetic. Select the 3 findings that argue most strongly against it.

options.text: EtCO2 36 mm Hg by nasal cannula

rationale.short: A normal EtCO2, no muscle rigidity and a normal potassium argue against malignant hyperthermia (CK often rises hours later, so an early normal CK is weaker evidence). Fever, tachycardia and hot sweaty skin occur in both; incision pain does not help.

a.text: Key. MH breaks down muscle cells, and potassium rises early with the acidosis; a normal potassium with a temperature of 39.6 °C argues against it.

b.text: Not a key. Occurs in both conditions.

c.text: Not a key. Occurs in both.

d.text: Key. Malignant hyperthermia causes a rising EtCO2 early; a normal value argues against it.

e.text: Not a key. Occurs in both.

f.text: Not a key. Neutral; does not help tell the two apart.

g.text: Key. MH usually causes muscle rigidity, often starting in the jaw.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 3 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 3 choices. Maximum 3. Example: choosing 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Rising EtCO2 and rigidity point to MH; their absence points elsewhere.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA/RRP: differentiate perioperative hyperthermia. Trap: reflex dantrolene.

items.stem: Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{c}}, as shown by {{e}}.

options.text: fever and rapid AF in a client with untreated Graves disease
agitation and disorientation soon after anesthesia
a temperature of 39.6 °C within hours of sevoflurane
a loose stool and fever after an appendectomy

rationale.short: Thyroid storm: fever, rapid AF and confusion after surgery in a client who stopped methimazole 3 months ago.

c.text: (a) ‘emergence delirium’: Not a key. Does not cause fever of 39.6 °C or AF at 156/min. (b) ‘thyroid storm’: Key. Untreated Graves with fever, rapid AF and confusion after surgery. (c) ‘malignant hyperthermia’: Not a key. EtCO2, muscle tone, potassium and CK are normal. (d) ‘sepsis from the appendix’: Not a key. Uncomplicated appendicitis; this onset is too fast.

e.text: (a) ‘fever and rapid AF in a client with untreated Graves disease’: Key. Surgery triggered a storm in untreated hyperthyroidism. (b) ‘agitation and disorientation soon after anesthesia’: Not a key. Emergence delirium does not explain fever, AF and a free T4 of 5.8 ng/dL. (c) ‘a temperature of 39.6 °C within hours of sevoflurane’: Not a key. Fever after a volatile agent raises concern for MH, but EtCO2, muscle tone and CK are normal. (d) ‘a loose stool and fever after an appendectomy’: Not a key. Could suggest infection, but the appendicitis was uncomplicated and onset is too fast; diarrhea is also a storm sign.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: Rationale (dyad) scoring: 1 point only when both the condition and its evidence are correct. A correct condition with the wrong evidence earns 0 of 1.
expanded.takeaway: Surgery can trigger a storm in untreated Graves disease.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize the hypothesis. Trap: emergence delirium.

items.stem: Is each intervention indicated for this client?

rows.text: Beta-blocker (propranolol)
Propylthiouracil (PTU)
Iodine given before the thionamide
Aspirin for the fever
Dantrolene
Hydrocortisone IV
Cooling blanket

rationale.short: Propranolol, PTU, hydrocortisone and cooling are indicated. Iodine before the thionamide, aspirin and dantrolene are not.

r1.text: Indicated. Controls HR and adrenergic symptoms.

r2.text: Indicated. Blocks new hormone production.

r3.text: Not indicated. Iodine first can fuel more hormone production; give it at least 1 hour after PTU.

r4.text: Not indicated. Salicylates free more thyroid hormone from proteins.

r5.text: Not indicated. For malignant hyperthermia, which is not supported here.

r6.text: Indicated. Blocks T4-to-T3 conversion and covers possible adrenal insufficiency.

expanded.takeaway: Storm care: block the effects (beta-blocker), block production (PTU), then block release (iodine).

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1245 prescriptions. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: If the BP before the 1645 propranolol dose is 96/58 mm Hg, the nurse should {{d1}}. PTU is sometimes chosen over methimazole in thyroid storm because PTU {{d2}}. The nurse checks fingerstick glucose more often after the hydrocortisone because {{d3}}.

options.text: hold the dose and notify the HCP
give the dose and recheck the BP in 1 hour
also blocks the conversion of T4 to T3
is given once a day, so doses are not missed
stops the gland from releasing its stored hormone
carries no risk of liver injury
potassium iodide causes low blood glucose

rationale.short: Hold propranolol for an SBP below 100 mm Hg and notify the HCP. PTU is sometimes chosen because it also blocks T4-to-T3 conversion, although either thionamide is acceptable. High-dose hydrocortisone raises glucose, so check it more often.

d1.text: (a) ‘give half the dose’: Not a key. The nurse cannot change the dose without a prescription. (b) ‘give the dose as prescribed’: Not a key. Ignores the hold parameter; propranolol can drop the BP further. (c) ‘hold the dose and notify the HCP’: Key. The prescription says to hold for SBP below 100 mm Hg. (d) ‘give the dose and recheck the BP in 1 hour’: Not a key. Ignores the hold parameter.

d2.text: (a) ‘also blocks the conversion of T4 to T3’: Key. This extra action can lower active hormone faster. Current consensus (ETA-endorsed 2026 joint statement; outcome data show no clear advantage) accepts either PTU or high-dose methimazole in a storm. (b) ‘is given once a day, so doses are not missed’: Not a key. It is given every 4 hours here. (c) ‘stops the gland from releasing its stored hormone’: Not a key. That is the action of iodine. (d) ‘carries no risk of liver injury’: Not a key. PTU has a boxed warning for liver injury.

d3.text: (a) ‘PTU lowers blood glucose’: Not a key. PTU does not cause hypoglycemia. (b) ‘acetaminophen raises blood glucose’: Not a key. Acetaminophen does not raise glucose. (c) ‘potassium iodide causes low blood glucose’: Not a key. Iodine does not affect glucose. (d) ‘glucocorticoids raise blood glucose’: Key. High-dose hydrocortisone causes stress-level hyperglycemia.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Apply hold parameters, know why PTU is chosen, and watch glucose on stress-dose steroids.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PHA: apply hold parameters and anticipate drug effects. Trap: giving a beta-blocker through a low BP.

r1.text: Shows improvement. Rate and rhythm controlled.

r2.text: Needs follow-up now. Possible heart failure from the storm; report. The HCP may reassess the beta-blocker (for example, switch to titratable IV esmolol) if thyrotoxic heart failure is suspected.

r3.text: Shows improvement. Fever has resolved with acetaminophen and cooling.

r4.text: Needs follow-up now. High after hydrocortisone and stress; report and monitor.

r5.text: Shows improvement. Confusion resolved.

r6.text: Needs follow-up now. Still tachypneic while the HR and temperature have come down, and now with new crackles and lower SpO2.

cases.title: Oncology unit: confused and vomiting

patient.history: Small cell lung cancer, diagnosed 3 weeks ago; first chemotherapy cycle in 3 days. Poor appetite; lost 5 kg in 2 months. Former smoker. No diuretics or other home medications. Admitted last night for weakness. Full code.

entries.text: Admission 2200: Alert, oriented x 4. Mild headache. Chronic cough. Mucous membranes moist. No edema. Lungs: diminished right upper lobe (known tumor).

0950: Laboratory called a critical sodium of 118 mEq/L (drawn at 0900) to the nurse. 1000: Daughter reports her mother 'isn't herself.' Oriented to person, not place or time. Headache 6/10. Vomited once at 0930. Mucous membranes moist. No edema. No orthostatic changes. Lungs unchanged from admission. Chronic cough.
1030: HCP notified; prescriptions entered (see Orders). 3% saline 100 mL bolus given 1040-1050.

Next day 0215: 3% saline stopped per order (sodium 124 at 0200); HCP notified. 0530: Alert, oriented x 4. Headache resolved. No vomiting since 0930 yesterday. No seizure activity. Hourly urine output: 0300 90 mL, 0400 150 mL, 0500 300 mL; urine pale. 0500 sodium and urine osmolality just resulted.

tabs.label: Laboratory Results
rows: 50-1,200 mOsm/kg (expected below 100 when serum is low)
No fixed range; interpret with volume status (mEq/L)

entries.text: 1030: 3% sodium chloride 100 mL IV over 10 minutes now; may repeat x 2 for seizure or worsening confusion. Then 3% sodium chloride 0.5 mL/kg/h; stop the infusion when sodium reaches 124 mEq/L (a rise of 6) and notify HCP. Sodium every 4 hours. Goal: raise sodium 4-6 mEq/L in 24 hours; do not exceed 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO twice daily. Fluid restriction 1,000 mL/day. Strict intake and output. Seizure precautions. Notify HCP for urine output above 100 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours or sodium rise of 6 mEq/L or more in any 12 hours.

references.locator: hyponatremia management: 100 mL 3% bolus up to 3 times for severe symptoms; continuous 0.5-2 mL/kg/h for moderate symptoms; goal 4-6, limit 8 mEq/L/24 h in high ODS risk
high-risk limit 8 mEq/L/24 h; re-lowering with D5W and desmopressin after overcorrection

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1000 findings. Click to highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

tokens.text: Oriented to person, not place or time

rationale.short: New confusion, a worse headache, vomiting and a sodium of 118 need action now. Moist membranes, no edema, chronic cough, normal BP and normal glucose do not.

h2.text: Key. Worse than on admission; a sign of brain swelling.

h3.text: Key. A sign of moderately severe hyponatremia.

h4.text: Key. Severe and lower than 131 a week ago.

h5.text: Not a key. Euvolemic; supports a diagnosis but needs no action.

h9.text: Not a key. Normal; rules out a falsely low sodium from high glucose.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Recognize cues: compare each finding with the client's baseline and expected values; flag what is new, abnormal and dangerous.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 4. Example: selecting 3 keys and 1 distractor earns 3 - 1 = 2 of 4.
expanded.takeaway: Low sodium plus new brain symptoms is an emergency.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: recognize electrolyte emergencies. Trap: blaming confusion on cancer or age.

items.stem: The HCP suspects the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Which findings support this suspicion or point to its cause? Select all that apply.

rationale.short: Low serum osmolality, concentrated urine, high urine sodium and euvolemia support SIADH, and small cell lung cancer is its likely cause. The potassium and the temperature do not support it.

a.text: Key. The urine is concentrated even though the blood is dilute: ADH is acting.

b.text: Not a key. Normal; it neither supports SIADH nor points to a cause.

c.text: Not a key. Low potassium is not part of SIADH; here it reflects poor intake and matters as a risk factor for osmotic demyelination.

d.text: Key. A common source of ectopic ADH.

e.text: Key. Euvolemia fits SIADH.

f.text: Key. The kidneys keep excreting sodium.

g.text: Key. Low: the blood is diluted.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Analyze cues: link each cue to the condition it best explains, and ask what else could explain it.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 5. Example: selecting 4 keys and 1 distractor earns 4 - 1 = 3 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: SIADH = dilute blood, concentrated urine, normal volume.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: interpret labs. Trap: low potassium as an SIADH sign.

items.stem: Select the 2 client problems that are the highest priority to plan care around now.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about the chemotherapy that is planned in 3 days
Osmotic demyelination if the sodium is corrected too fast
Ineffective airway clearance from her cough
Hypokalemia with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L
Risk for seizures from brain swelling

rationale.short: Seizure risk now and brain injury from overcorrection are the priorities. She is not volume depleted, and potassium is a risk factor to fix, not the main threat.

a.text: Not a key. Important later.

b.text: Key. Her low potassium and weight loss raise the risk, so the safe limit is 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

c.text: Not a key. Chronic cough without distress.

d.text: Not a key. She is euvolemic; one episode of vomiting.

e.text: Not a key. Needs replacing, but its main danger here is as a risk factor for osmotic demyelination, already captured in that problem.

f.text: Key. Sodium 118 with confusion and vomiting.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Prioritize hypotheses: rank the possible problems by how fast each could harm the client (ABCs, unstable over stable, actual over potential).
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 2 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 2 choices. Maximum 2. Example: choosing 1 keys and 1 distractor earns 1 of 2.
expanded.takeaway: Hyponatremia has two dangers: too low now, and corrected too fast later.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: prioritize. Trap: forgetting overcorrection risk.

items.stem: Which actions should the nurse plan to take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage 3 L of oral fluids daily
Plan sodium checks during hypertonic saline
Raise the sodium to 135 mEq/L within 24 hours
Keep strict intake and output records
Restrict dietary salt to 2 g daily

rationale.short: Seizure precautions, frequent sodium checks and strict I&O. Normal saline boluses, extra fluids, correcting to 135 in a day and salt restriction are wrong.

a.text: Not a key. Free water worsens SIADH.

b.text: Key. Checks at 2- to 4-hour intervals catch a rise that is too fast.

c.text: Key. Severe hyponatremia can cause seizures.

d.text: Not a key. Far too fast; limit 8 mEq/L in 24 hours for her.

e.text: Key. A sudden rise in urine output signals rapid correction.

f.text: Not a key. She needs salt, not less of it.

g.text: Not a key. In SIADH with concentrated urine, normal saline can lower sodium further.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Generate solutions: list actions that treat the priority problem; drop anything unsafe, outdated or outside RN scope.
expanded.pointsLost: +/- scoring: +1 for each correct selection, -1 for each incorrect selection, total never below 0. Maximum 3. Example: selecting 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 - 1 = 1 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: In SIADH: no free water, careful hypertonic saline, frequent sodium checks.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA/SAF: plan electrolyte care. Trap: '0.9% saline for low sodium.'

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1030 prescriptions. Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

payload.template: After the bolus, the nurse sets the 3% saline infusion at {{d1}}. In the first 24 hours the sodium should not rise above {{d2}}. The nurse should notify the HCP if {{d3}}.

options.text: BP stays near 128/76 mm Hg, as on admission
urine output tops 100 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours
sodium rises by 2 mEq/L over the first 4 hours

rationale.short: 0.5 × 61 = 31 mL/h. The 24-hour limit is 118 + 8 = 126. Report urine output above 100 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours because a water diuresis can overcorrect sodium.

d1.text: (a) ‘15 mL/h’: Not a key. Uses 0.25 mL/kg. (b) ‘31 mL/h’: Key. 0.5 mL × 61 kg = 30.5, rounded to 31 mL/h. (c) ‘100 mL/h’: Not a key. Confuses the bolus with the infusion. (d) ‘61 mL/h’: Not a key. Uses 1 mL/kg.

d2.text: (a) ‘122 mEq/L’: Not a key. A rise of 4 is the low end of the goal, not the limit. (b) ‘126 mEq/L’: Key. 118 + 8 = 126. (c) ‘130 mEq/L’: Not a key. A rise of 12; too fast for her. (d) ‘135 mEq/L’: Not a key. Normal, but far too fast.

d3.text: (a) ‘BP stays near 128/76 mm Hg, as on admission’: Not a key. Normal. (b) ‘urine osmolality stays above 500 mOsm/kg’: Not a key. Expected in SIADH early on. (c) ‘urine output tops 100 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours’: Key. A water diuresis can raise sodium too fast. (d) ‘sodium rises by 2 mEq/L over the first 4 hours’: Not a key. Expected and on track.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Take action: carry out the plan in a safe order, within scope and per the prescription or protocol.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each drop-down earns 1 point when correct; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 3. Example: one wrong drop-down earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: Know the ceiling (start + 8) and the warning sign (sudden diuresis).
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PHA: calculate rates and limits. Trap: using 1 mL/kg or targeting a normal sodium.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the next-morning findings at 0530. For each finding, specify whether it shows improvement or needs action now. Choose one column for each finding: if a finding calls for any action now, choose 'Needs action now'.

rows.text: Alert, oriented x 4, headache resolved
No seizure activity and no further vomiting
Sodium 127 mEq/L at 0500 (118 at 0900 yesterday)
Urine output 90, then 150, then 300 mL/h; urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg (520 yesterday)
Potassium 3.6 mEq/L (3.2 yesterday)

rationale.short: Her symptoms and potassium have improved, but sodium rose 9 mEq/L in 20 hours (over the limit of 8 in 24 hours) during a dilute water diuresis. Report the sodium and the urine output now.

r1.text: Shows improvement. Brain symptoms resolved.

r2.text: Shows improvement. Symptoms resolved.

r3.text: Needs action now. A rise of 9 in 20 hours exceeds her limit of 8 in 24 hours: report now. The HCP may re-lower the sodium with D5W and desmopressin.

r4.text: Needs action now. A dilute water diuresis: ADH has switched off. Output above 100 mL/h for 2 consecutive hours meets the notify rule, and the free-water loss will keep raising the sodium unless the HCP intervenes.

r5.text: Shows improvement. Replaced; note that potassium replacement also raises sodium.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Evaluate outcomes: compare new data with the earlier timepoint; decide what improved, what did not and what needs action now.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 5. Example: one wrong row earns 4 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: Improvement in symptoms does not mean safe correction: check the rate of rise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA/PHA: evaluate correction. Trap: celebrating the higher sodium.

standalone.stem: Complete the diagram. Choose the condition the client most likely has, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Have the client walk to strengthen contractions
Insert a large-bore IV and send a type and crossmatch
Place the client in the Trendelenburg position
Notify the obstetric team of possible emergency birth
Give nifedipine to stop the contractions and delay birth

exhibit.title: Nurses' Notes, 35 weeks, 1415
exhibit.text: Client, 29 years old, G2 P1, 35 2/7 weeks, chronic hypertension treated with labetalol 200 mg PO twice daily. One prior vaginal birth; no uterine surgery. Ultrasound at 32 weeks: placenta on the back wall of the uterus, away from the cervix. At 1340 sudden, constant abdominal and back pain, 8/10. Small amount of dark red vaginal bleeding (pad weighed 40 g; dry pad weight 10 g). Uterus firm and tender between contractions. Contractions every 2 minutes, low amplitude. FHR baseline 165/min, minimal variability, recurrent late decelerations. Maternal HR 112/min, BP 158/98 mm Hg, RR 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, T 37.0 °C. Platelets 132 ×10³/µL (reference 150-400). Fibrinogen 210 mg/dL (reference 300-600 in pregnancy).

rationale.short: Abruption: constant pain, a firm tender uterus, dark bleeding and late decelerations with hypertension. Call the team for possible birth and prepare IV access and blood. Monitor the FHR, fibrinogen and platelets.

c1.text: Key. Constant pain, a firm tender uterus, dark bleeding and fetal distress in a client with hypertension.

c2.text: Not a key. No uterine scar and not in labor with oxytocin.

c3.text: Not a key. Labor does not cause a constantly firm, tender uterus with fetal distress.

c4.text: Not a key. The placenta is away from the cervix, and previa bleeding is painless.

a1.text: Not a key. Unsafe with active bleeding and fetal distress; she needs side-lying rest and monitoring.

a2.text: Key. Prepares for hemorrhage and transfusion.

a3.text: Not a key. Outdated; side-lying is used.

a4.text: Key. Fetal distress with an abruption usually means prompt birth.

a5.text: Not a key. Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with fetal distress.

m1.text: Not a key. Not a useful marker here.

m2.text: Key. Continuous EFM shows whether the fetus is tolerating the abruption.

m3.text: Not a key. Repeated exams do not track the threat.

m4.text: Not a key. Not affected by abruption.

m5.text: Key. Both are already falling; abruption is a leading cause of DIC.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Bow-tie: the condition in the middle must explain every cue; then pick actions that treat it and parameters that show the treatment worked.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring per slot: 1 condition + 2 actions + 2 parameters = maximum 5. Action and parameter choices may go in either of their two slots. Example: the right condition, 1 right action and 2 right parameters earn 4 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: Painful bleeding plus a firm uterus = abruption; watch for DIC.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: manage antepartum emergencies. Trap: Trendelenburg and tocolysis myths.

standalone.stem: Complete the diagram. Choose the condition the client most likely has, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Call for the emergency cesarean birth team
Lift the presenting part off the cervix with a gloved hand
Apply fundal pressure to speed the birth

exhibit.title: Labor Flowsheet and Nurses' Notes, 2140
exhibit.text: Client, 33 years old, G2 P1, 39 4/7 weeks, trial of labor after 1 prior low-transverse cesarean. Oxytocin at 8 milliunits/min for augmentation. Epidural in place since 1900 with good pain relief. At 2125: cervix 7 cm, station 0, contractions every 2-3 minutes. At 2138 the client cries out with sudden sharp abdominal pain 'like something tore,' felt through the epidural. Contractions have stopped on the monitor. FHR: prolonged deceleration to 70/min for 4 minutes. Presenting part now at -3 station. Small amount of bright red vaginal bleeding. Maternal HR 124/min, BP 92/54 mm Hg, RR 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air.

rationale.short: Uterine rupture: sudden tearing pain, contractions stop, the presenting part rises and the FHR drops. Stop oxytocin and call the cesarean team; monitor the FHR and maternal HR and BP.

c1.text: Key. Sudden pain through an epidural, loss of station, contractions stopping and a prolonged deceleration during TOLAC.

c2.text: Not a key. Prolapse causes FHR changes but not pain, loss of station or maternal hypotension.

c3.text: Not a key. Abruption causes a firm, contracting uterus; it does not cause loss of station.

c4.text: Not a key. Transition increases contractions; here they stopped.

a1.text: Key. Rupture needs surgery within minutes.

a2.text: Key. Oxytocin stresses the torn uterus.

a3.text: Not a key. Would worsen the tear and the bleeding.

a4.text: Not a key. A cord-prolapse action; the presenting part has already moved up.

a5.text: Not a key. Can extend the rupture.

m1.text: Not a key. Not relevant once surgery is needed.

m3.text: Not a key. Used for magnesium or preeclampsia, not rupture.

m4.text: Key. Shows fetal oxygenation until birth.

m5.text: Not a key. Contractions have stopped; tracking them does not guide care.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Bow-tie: the condition in the middle must explain every cue; then pick actions that treat it and parameters that show the treatment worked.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring per slot: 1 condition + 2 actions + 2 parameters = maximum 5. Action and parameter choices may go in either of their two slots. Example: the right condition, 1 right action and 2 right parameters earn 4 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: During TOLAC, a sudden FHR drop with loss of station is rupture until proven otherwise.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: manage intrapartum emergencies. Trap: thinking stopped contractions mean the labor is resting.

standalone.stem: Complete the diagram. Choose the condition the client most likely has, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

options.text: Give 50% dextrose IV to protect the brain
Give aspirin 325 mg by mouth now to limit the clot
Give an IV BP drug per protocol to reach below 185/110 mm Hg
Lower the BP to below 140/90 mm Hg as fast as possible
Keep the client NPO until a swallow screen is passed
Deep tendon reflexes in the arms and legs

exhibit.title: ED Triage and Nurses' Notes, 1625
exhibit.text: Client, 55 years old, 82 kg, no known allergies, no medications, no prior stroke. Sudden inability to speak and right-sided weakness at 1530 while watching television; family called 911. Arrived 1605. Last known well 1530. NIHSS 10: aphasia, right facial droop, right arm and leg drift. BP 198/112 mm Hg (repeat 196/110), HR 86/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.9 °C. POC glucose 104 mg/dL (repeat 108). CT head: no hemorrhage. Code stroke activated; stroke team at bedside and preparing IV thrombolysis.

rationale.short: Acute ischemic stroke: sudden focal deficits, normal glucose, no hemorrhage. Lower BP below 185/110 before thrombolysis and keep the client NPO. Monitor BP and the NIHSS.

c1.text: Not a key. Causes headache, confusion and papilledema, not sudden one-sided weakness with aphasia.

c2.text: Key. Sudden focal deficits with a normal glucose and no hemorrhage on CT.

c3.text: Not a key. No seizure was witnessed; deficits started abruptly while watching television.

c4.text: Not a key. Glucose is 104 and 108 mg/dL.

a1.text: Not a key. Glucose is normal; extra dextrose can worsen outcomes.

a2.text: Not a key. Aspirin is held before thrombolysis and the client is NPO.

options.text: Minor thermal burn of the hand
Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring
Keep LR at the rate calculated from the 4% TBSA skin burn, regardless of urine output
Titrate LR to a urine output of 75-100 mL/h
Give furosemide to clear the dark urine
Discharge after the ECG if it is normal

exhibit.title: ED Nurses' Notes, 1010
exhibit.text: Client, 34 years old, 90 kg, electrical lineworker. Contact with a 7,200-volt line at 0935; thrown 2 meters. Small charred contact wounds on the right palm and the sole of the left foot. Estimated skin burn 4% TBSA. Severe pain in both thighs, 8/10. Urine tea-colored on first void (80 mL). Alert and oriented. HR 104/min, BP 138/84 mm Hg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air. ECG: sinus tachycardia with occasional PVCs. CK 6,400 U/L (reference 30-200).

rationale.short: High-voltage injury: small skin wounds hide deep muscle damage (thigh pain, tea-colored urine, CK 6,400). Monitor the heart continuously and run LR to a urine output of 75-100 mL/h until the urine clears.

c1.text: Key. Contact wounds on a hand and a foot, thigh pain, tea-colored urine and a high CK despite a small skin burn.

c2.text: Not a key. The skin burn is small, but the deep injury is not.

c3.text: Not a key. PVCs after high voltage are a cardiac effect of the current, not a coronary blockage.

c4.text: Not a key. Tea-colored urine here follows muscle injury, not trauma to the bladder.

a1.text: Key. Current through the body can cause dysrhythmias.

a2.text: Not a key. Skin TBSA underestimates electrical injury; the rate is titrated to urine output.

a3.text: Key. High flow flushes myoglobin until the urine clears.

a4.text: Not a key. Diuretics are not indicated for rhabdomyolysis; volume is.

a5.text: Not a key. Dysrhythmias and muscle injury can declare later.

m3.text: Not a key. Not the priority measure.

m4.text: Key. Shows whether myoglobin is clearing and the rate is enough.

m5.text: Not a key. The skin wound is not the main injury.

standalone.stem: The nurse reviews the client's trend at the day 12 clinic visit. Select the 3 instructions the nurse should give the client now.

options.text: Avoid anyone who is sick, including the grandchild if he or she gets ill
Call right away for a temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher
Take acetaminophen for a fever and call if the fever lasts more than a day
Check your temperature rectally for accuracy
Expect the counts to keep falling for the rest of the cycle
Have everyone at home clean their hands often
Wait until day 21 to report any new symptoms

exhibit.title: Laboratory Results: CBC With Differential
exhibit.note: Client, 71-year-old woman, lymphoma, cycle 1 of R-CHOP; pegfilgrastim 6 mg subcutaneous given on day 2 (prophylaxis, age over 65). Lives with spouse and a 6-year-old grandchild who attends school. Temperature today 36.8 °C. References: WBC 4.5-11.0 ×10³/µL; ANC 1,500-8,000/µL; hemoglobin 12.0-15.5 g/dL; platelets 150-400 ×10³/µL.

rationale.short: The ANC has fallen to 400/µL at the expected nadir, even with pegfilgrastim, which shortens neutropenia but does not prevent it. Teach her to call for a temperature of 38.0 °C or higher, to have the household clean hands often and to avoid sick contacts.

a.text: Key. Limits exposure while the ANC is lowest; a healthy grandchild does not need to be avoided.

b.text: Key. Fever during the nadir is an emergency; do not wait.

c.text: Not a key. Delays care and masks fever.

d.text: Not a key. Rectal routes are avoided in neutropenia.

e.text: Not a key. Washed produce is generally allowed; strict 'neutropenic diets' are not supported.

f.text: Not a key. The nadir is usually around days 7-12, then counts recover.

g.text: Key. Hand hygiene, especially before touching the client, is the best way to prevent infection.

h.text: Not a key. Symptoms are reported when they happen.

expanded.cjmmCoaching: Trend: read across the timepoints; the direction and rate of change matter more than any single value.
expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each of your 3 selections earns 1 point if it is a key; nothing is subtracted, and the screen blocks more than 3 choices. Maximum 3. Example: choosing 2 keys and 1 distractor earns 2 of 3.
expanded.takeaway: The nadir is the danger window: fever means call now.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan HPM: teach self-care at home. Trap: 'take acetaminophen and wait.'

exhibit.title: Burn Resuscitation Flowsheet (injury at 1200; 8 years old, 26 kg, 24% TBSA partial- and full-thickness)
exhibit.note: LR started at 1215 on arrival in the ED at 117 mL/h (3 mL x 26 kg x 24% = 1,872 mL per 24 h; 1,872 / 16 = 117 mL/h; the 24-hour count starts at the time of injury, 1200). D5LR maintenance at 66 mL/h by the 4-2-1 rule (4x10 + 2x10 + 1x6); maintenance is not titrated. Unit protocol for a child 30 kg or less: urine output goal 1 mL/kg/h. Each hour, if urine output is below 0.75 mL/kg/h, increase the LR rate by 10-20%; if 0.75-1.25 mL/kg/h, keep the rate; if above 1.25 mL/kg/h, decrease the LR rate by 10-20%. References: HR 70-110/min at rest for this age (higher expected with pain and hypovolemia).

rationale.short: Divide each urine output by 26 kg: 0.46 and 0.69 mL/kg/h are below the band, so increase; 1.04 and 1.08 are in the band, so keep; 1.77 is above, so decrease. The formula only sets the 117 mL/h starting rate.

r1.text: Increase the LR rate. 12 / 26 = 0.46 mL/kg/h, below 0.75; perfusion is poor (cap refill 4 s). Increase 117 mL/h by 20% to about 140 mL/h. Note: LR started 15 minutes after injury; giving half of 1,872 mL over the remaining 7.75 hours would be 936 / 7.75 = 120.8 mL/h, but the protocol uses the /16 starting rate (117 mL/h) and titrates to urine output.

r2.text: Increase the LR rate. 18 / 26 = 0.69 mL/kg/h, still below 0.75. Increase about 10%, to about 154 mL/h.

r3.text: Maintain the LR rate. 27 / 26 = 1.04 mL/kg/h, in the 0.75-1.25 band; keep about 154 mL/h.

r4.text: Maintain the LR rate. 28 / 26 = 1.08 mL/kg/h, still in the band; keep the rate.

r5.text: Decrease the LR rate. 46 / 26 = 1.77 mL/kg/h, above 1.25; decrease 10-20% to avoid over-resuscitation (fluid creep).

expanded.pointsLost: 0/1 scoring: each row earns 1 point when the correct column is chosen; nothing is subtracted. Maximum 5. Example: one wrong row earns 4 of 5.
expanded.takeaway: In burn resuscitation the urine output decides the next hour's rate.
expanded.whyItMatters: Test plan PA: pediatric burn titration. Trap: running the formula unchanged for 8 hours.
